 The stock market is offering no respite from a prolonged slump, casting a shadow over investors’ Diwali celebrations. Two years have passed since a stunning multi-year rally came to a halt. Intermittent rebounds have proved short-lived amid despondency over geopolitical tensions, inflationary pressures from soaring energy prices, a hawkish shift in monetary policy, and more. The correction in individual stocks has been steeper than what the headline index fall suggests.
For most lay investors, this is uncharted territory. But for the market mavens at India’s mutual fund companies, this is hunting season.
Even as pessimism grips the broader market, these fund manag ers are seeing fertile ground for finding new investable opportunities as well as compelling entry points for high-conviction names. In this 13th edition of our special Most Wanted Stocks feature, we have zeroed in on a few stocks that have been consistently favoured by fund managers. The six stocks we have shortlisted have seen a gradual rise in mutual fund holdings for four consecutive quarters since September 2025. For a detailed look at how we zeroed in on these names, refer to the methodology on page 7.
Keep in mind that mimicking fund managers’ big moves comes with caveats. They often build positions gradually at lower valua tions and exit swiftly when market conditions or fundamentals change. Investors should do their own due diligence and invest only surplus money they won’t need for the next few years.
 Live Events
 Fund managers’ favourite stocks 
 KFin Technologies
KFintech mainly serves the operational needs of as set managers with clients spanning mutual funds, alternative investment funds (AIFs), pension funds, and wealth managers. In its MF business, revenue growth has been slower amid a shift towards lower-yield liquid funds and a provision for an upcoming contract renewal. The management is keen on expanding the addressable market and diversifying revenue mix by reduc ing the contribution of domestic MF business to around 50% over the next three years.
The international business segment has seen several large deal wins as the company shifted its strategy from focusing on small boutique managers to large clients. With the integration of Singapore-based Ascent Funds Services (acquired recently), the management expects better yields and profitability led by new client wins and improving asset under management (AUM) growth in the Southeast Asian business.
The company has undertaken several cost optimisation measures which is expected to help deliver 40% Ebitda (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization) margin for FY27. Structural tailwinds in the MF industry, coupled with increasing diversification into international, issuer solutions, alternates and pension busi nesses, are expected to drive KFin’s long-term growth.
 Note: "Its technology-led, asset-light platform model, improving global fund administration capabilities position the company well to capitalise on opportunities across both Indian and global markets.”
 MOTILAL OSWAL 
FINANCIAL SERVICES

 Rainbow Children’s Medicare
Rainbow Children’s Medicare (Rainbow) is one of India’s largest multi-speciality pediatric and perinatal hospital chains, operating in a niche, underpenetrated segment. According to analysts, Rainbow’s evolution from a pediatric-focused hospital chain into a comprehensive mother-and-child healthcare platform enables patients to remain within the Rainbow ecosystem throughout different stages of the care journey. This integrated model not only strengthens patient acquisition, enhances patient retention, improves referral networks but also supports higher lifetime value per patient. These structural advantages have translated into industry leading margins, healthy returns on capital and a net cash balance sheet.
The management expects revenue to double over the next four years, with plans to double its capacity in the next five years. Rainbow’s leadership position in the pediatric market is further strengthened by its foray into high-growth non-core markets (North and West India), which should aid revenue trajectory. Expected occupancy improvement and investments in strengthening tech should further provide revenue visibility.
However, the initial drag from new projects may weigh on profitability in the near term. Analysts believe Rainbow’s differentiated business model is difficult to replicate, creating a sustainable competitive advantage.
 Note :"Rainbow is well positioned to capitalise on the long-term growth opportunity in India’s under-penetrated pediatric and maternal healthcare market.”

 Indus Towers , India’s largest mobile tower infrastructure company, has strong order visibility for the next 3-4 quarters, driven by network expansion and migration of expiring tenancies from rival tower operators.
Relief on Vodafone Idea’s (VI) adjusted gross revenue (AGR) dues, allowing reduced and deferred payouts, has eased concerns over a key tenant’s continuity. It frees up VI’s cash flow for network upgrades and 5G rollout, giving Indus, its preferred network expansion partner, greater visibility on incremental tenancy additions.

docs.title: Sebi to delist penny stocks: Market regulator plans AI-based surveillance of such firms
docs.text:
The Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) will delist companies with no economic activity from stock exchanges to protect investors, particularly those who invest in penny stocks.
 “These companies pose a potential danger to investors, and therefore, it is necessary to remove them from the listed space. We are making efforts towards their delisting,” Sebi chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey said Saturday in Kolkata.
Several companies with no economic activity remain listed, potentially creating scope for market manipulation.
Such firms could pose a danger and should not continue to crowd the listed space, Pandey said.
Investors with limited knowledge of the stock market tend to buy penny stocks because they are available at throwaway prices, often below Rs 10 or Rs 20. They risk losing money when prices correct.
 Live Events
According to an ET report on November 1, as many as 10 penny stocks saw their prices fall 35-70% over the past three months.
The market regulator is planning to use an artificial intelligence-based system to monitor companies with minimal economic activity and generate alerts faster, Pandey said.
He also said Sebi is likely to issue its proposed consultation paper on compliance requirements for foreign institutional investors (FIIs) within weeks. The regulator will also take a consultative approach to capacity building for independent directors.
The consultation paper on FIIs will seek views on aligning Indian norms with global standards. This comes amid large outflows of foreign capital that have contributed to a persistent decline in stock indices.
 Foreign portfolio investors withdrew a net $31.4 billion from Indian equities in the first 10 months of the year, seeking higher returns in safe-haven assets amid rising US treasury yields, the dollar's relative strength against other major currencies and continued geopolitical uncertainty.

 With Diwali festivities peaking and the wedding season starting by month-end, the recent correction in gold prices may have come as a welcome opportunity for households considering traditional purchases. The 19.2% dip—from Rs.1.75 lakh per 10 gram peak on 29 January 2026 to Rs.1.41 lakh on 29 October (MCX Spot price, Bloomberg)—is significant because not only does it signal a reversal after a strong rally, but also because gold’s credentials as a safe-haven asset are being tested.
 “It has moved from being a conservative asset class to a volatile one because that’s how it has behaved in the past 3-4 years. The world has become unpredictable, where asset classes are being driven more by geopolitical factors, fear and greed, rather than their fundamentals and technicals,” says Kalpesh Asher, Founder, Full Circle Financial Planners and Advisors.
Currently, gold prices are being driven by a combination of factors, including monetary policy, real yields, geopolitical uncertainty, and investment demand. “The elevated United States inflation and changing US Federal Reserve rate expectations are keeping Treasury yields high and cre ating volatility in bullion, but central bank purchases, strong exchange-traded fund (ETF) flows, Chinese investment demand, and concerns around rising US debt continue to provide structural support,” says Manav Modi, Commodities Analyst, Motilal Oswal Financial Services . 
While the price uncertainty may persist, most experts believe the upswing is likely to continue in the short term. Should you make the most of the dips and buy gold for personal use or invest more this festive season?
 Outlook for gold
“The demand for gold has remained constructive in 2026 and this trend is likely to continue over the next 6-12 months,” says Vijay Kuppa, CEO, InCred Money. The demand for gold in the first half of 2026 rose by about 2% from the corresponding period a year ago, to 2,522 tonnes with a record value of $380 billion, according to the World Gold Council data.
 Live Events
Agrees Mahendra Luniya, Chairman, Vighnaharta Gold. “Gold prices could remain in the Rs.2-2.25 lakh range over the next 6-12 months because the current uncertainty is likely to increase. The US debt may continue to increase and the dollar is expected to remain strong up to a certain level. Beyond that point, political issues will have a greater influence on gold prices, which could lead to a further price rise,” he says.
However, some choppiness cannot be ruled out depending on factors such as the US Fed rate hikes and geopolitical risks. “The Fed resumed rate hikes in September, US bond yields are near their highest in about two decades, and the dollar has strengthened. That’s what pulled gold down from its peak. If the Fed continues to increase rates, gold could correct further,” he says.
 Should you buy now?
“Prior to 2023, the question was not whether to buy during the festive season or not, but in what form and how much to buy,” says Asher. “Indians still want to buy gold on festive occasions, but are more cautious and have an eye on the prices, instead of splurging blindly,” he adds.
Timing the market may not be the ideal way to decide gold purchase because it would depend on several factors, including your existing portfolio, financial goals and whether it’s for personal use or an investment. “Rather than making purchase decisions solely around short-term market movements, consumers should consider their financial objectives, planned expenditure and the purpose for which they intend to own gold,” says Samit Guha, Managing Director & CEO, MMTC-PAMP.
For those focused on investment rather than traditional purchase, it may be to allocate small amounts regularly through a systematic approach. “Investors should start to accumulate gold as there is no right bottom for any price. Since more volatility is warranted, a staggered approach is advised, with purchase recom mended at dips,” says Modi.
Kuppa agrees. “Gold is neither clearly overvalued, nor a bargain. It’s fairly priced if the US rates stop rising, and expensive if they don’t. That’s a bet on the Fed, which is why we suggest buying in stages and treating gold as a diversifier, not a trade,” says Kuppa.
Luniya, however, is more confident. “The current prices are attractive, and for those who want to remain invested for 2-5 years, they present a very good opportunity to invest and expect good returns,” he says. Still, he recommends consulting a financial adviser and your portfolio needs before making a decision.
 Before buying, consider the pros & cons of various types of gold 
 Consider these features to assess suitability 
 In what form should you buy?
The choice of gold ownership—physical, ETFs, mutual funds, digital, sovereign gold bonds, electronic gold receipts—depends on the consumer’s objective, preferred mode of access, and intended use. “Each format serves a different requirement, and consumers should understand the associated costs, liquidity arrangements, custody mechanisms, and applicable regulatory framework before deciding,” says Guha.
Most experts believe gold ETFs are the best choice if you want to buy gold as an investment. “With gold ETFs, you are free from the responsibility of physically storing and safeguarding gold. When gold prices rise, ETF prices also rise, allowing you to benefit from the hike,” says Luniya.
It may also be the default choice currently for those wanting to start investing in a systematic manner since investment in gold fund of funds (FoFs) has been temporarily restricted by the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi). “While no official reason has been conveyed, the mark

Brokerages issued mixed calls across metals and consumer stocks. While Motilal Oswal remains upbeat on Jindal Steel & Power and Gopal Snacks, citing strong growth visibility and margin improvement, Citi maintains a Sell on Hindustan Zinc despite supportive silver trends. Stock-specific fundamentals continue to shape differentiated outlooks.

Nifty ended Friday with sharp cuts amid selling pressure across the board, with consumer, IT and energy stocks dragging the markets the most. India VIX also moved back above its 200-DMA, indicating rising fear among the market participants. 
 Commenting on the technical charts, Rupak De, Senior Technical Analyst at LKP Securities, said that the setup has turned relatively cautious, with the index slipping below its 20-DMA for the first time in the past few sessions. Additionally, it has breached the 38.2% Fibonacci retracement of the prior up move from 24,571 to 26,341, he added. "With the index closing below the key support level of 25,500, the near-term bias appears weak, and there is potential for a decline toward the 25,000 mark in the short term. On the upside, immediate resistance is seen around 25,800," De said.
Here are 2 stock recommendations for Friday:
 Buy Kirloskar Oil Engines at Rs 1,375-1,385 | Upside: 5% | Target: Rs 1,500 | Stop Loss: Rs 1,320
 Kirloskar Oil Engines is currently taking a breakout of the rounding bottom formation on the daily time frame. The RSI is trending upward, reflecting positive momentum, and the stock finds support at the 21-day EMA, with all key EMAs rising. The stock is trading above important moving averages, indicating a bullish trend. 1,320 could work as an immediate support, and a hurdle can be seen at 1,500.
 (Drumil Vithlani, Technical Research Analyst, Bonanza Portfolio) 
 Buy Bajaj Finance at Rs 1,024-1,026 | Upside: 4% | Stop Loss: Rs 990 | Target: Rs 1,070
 Bajaj Finance is currently taking a breakout of the downward-moving channel on the daily time frame. The lower trend line has provided support, accompanied by the formation of a bullish candlestick pattern, indicating a potential short-term upward movement in the stock. Momentum Indicator RSI is trading near the overbought region, which confirms the bullishness in the script.

As preparations for the Union Budget 2026–27 gather pace, the groundwork underway signals a clear policy intent to accelerate domestic demand, revive private investment and generate employment, according to a budget note by Motilal Oswal Financial Services (MOFSL). The brokerage has identified five stocks across auto, agriculture, defence, financials and infrastructure themes, which it believes could deliver strong gains for investors.
 "The Budget is expected to focus on income-tax, GST, and customs simplification to enhance ease of doing business and support fiscal consolidation, alongside targeted support for agriculture, MSMEs, manufacturing, infrastructure, higher defence capex, EVs, and renewables through credit and incentives," the note authored by Research Analysts Sneha Poddar and Rekha Jaat said.
A strong capital expenditure thrust across highways, logistics, defence, rail freight corridors and connectivity is anticipated, complemented by emphasis on skilling, rural prosperity, women empowerment, AI adoption, climate action and digital finance to anchor India’s next phase of economic expansion, the note added.
The finance ministry started work on the Union Budget for 2026-27 from October 9 as per a circular issued by the Department of Economic Affairs (DEA).
The preparations come against the backdrop of an additional 50% US tariff on most Indian goods and other external headwinds. These have raised risks to India's growth and jobs outlook, prompting calls for stronger support to the export sector.
 Live Events
 5 stocks to buy: 
The stocks recommended by MOFSL are TVS Motor Company, UPL , Bharat Dynamics (BDL), M&M Financial Services and Dalmia Bharat , and each of these stocks has been assigned a 20% weight.
 1) TVS Motors: TVS Motors continues to outperform peers and is well-positioned to benefit from the budget’s push to boost domestic consumption and rural demand through higher allocations, income support, and infrastructure spending.
MOFSL said that improving rural sentiment, strong entry-level recovery and sustained two-wheeler demand will be key triggers. Moreover, the company's market share gains, easing discounts, and margin expansion will provide strong earnings visibility. The Apache and Ntorq maker remains its top pick in OEMs.
 2) UPL: The diversified agrochemical leader is well positioned to benefit from the union budget push riding on rural prosperity via higher agri credit, MSME support, and value-chain strengthening, lifting farmer incomes and crop-protection demand.
The company's strong points are stronger volumes, export tailwinds, improved working-capital discipline and post-bond-repayment balance-sheet strength, the brokerage note said. The company's rising focus on speciality chemicals supports solid 2HFY26 growth.
 3) Bharat Dynamics: Bharat Dynamics (BDL), a defence play, has a robust Rs 50,000 crore order pipeline over five years, with Rs 20,000 crore targeted in 2-3 years. This aligns with the expected defence capex surge and infra push.
The recent Rs 2.5 lakh crore DAC approvals for missiles, undersea warfare, and naval arms leverage BDL's tactical/strategic expertise, propelling FY31 turnover to Rs 100bn via indigenisation and lower provisions, the note said.
 4) M&M Financial Services: M&M Financial is poised for Union Budget 2026-27 benefits via rural prosperity, MSME credit, and employment focus, driving PV/tractor loan growth amid surging volumes from festive demand, GST cuts, and restocking.
The company targets Rs 3 lakh crore in assets under management (AUM) by 2030, which is at an 18-20% CAGR, bolstered by AI underwriting, lower credit costs, controlled opex, and margin stability for strong earnings visibility in retail portfolios.
 5) Dalmia Bharat: The cement company benefits from the budget’s infra capex surge, PMAY rural housing, and urban projects, driving cement volume growth.
Dalmia Bharat is a low-cost cement producer with high blending ratios, green power and low freight. The company is targeting 62 mtpa capacity by FY28, and its cost optimisation endeavours will likely lift EBITDA margins amid sector consolidation.

Reliance Power 's board of directors on Monday approved the issuance of up to 46.20 crore equity shares/warrants worth Rs 1,525 crore via preferential allotment mode.
 The board has set the issue price at Rs 33 per share.
The issue price of equity shares/warrants is at a discount of 13% over Monday's closing price of Rs 38.15 on the NSE. The announcement was made after market hours and Reliance Power shares on Monday ended with gains of Rs 1.81 or 4.98% over the previous closing price.
 Reliance Infrastructure Limited, the promoter of the company, will enhance its equity stake by over Rs 600 crore, a company filing said. The other investors in the preferential issue are Authum Investment and Infrastructure Limited and Sanatan Financial Advisory Services Private Limited.
The proceeds from the preferential issue will be utilised to expand business operations directly and/or through investment in subsidiaries and joint ventures, debt reduction and for general corporate purposes, the filing said.

The markets worldwide are waiting with bated breath on what will be a historic policy announcement from the US Federal Reserve , where the central bank is expected to usher in a rate cut cycle.
 The announcement will be made at 11:30 pm IST (Indian Standard Time) on Wednesday.
If analysts are to be believed, the US Fed is all but certain to cut interest rates for the first time in more than four years.
However, there is no consensus on the quantum of reduction. Some are predicting a smaller cut of a quarter of a percentage point, while others believe a bigger half-point reduction is in the works.
Senior officials at the US central bank, including Powell, have indicated that a rate cut is coming, as inflation eases toward the bank's long-term target of 2%, and the labour market continues to cool in the post-Covid economy.
 Live Events
If the Fed starts the rate cut cycle, the Reserve Bank of India is also expected to follow suit.
A smaller cut would be a more predictable move, while a bigger cut would do more to boost demand — while also running the risk of reigniting inflation.
 WATCH LIVE TODAY: Press conference with #FOMC Chair Powell at 2:30 p.m. ET: https://t.co/1uJrua5qsH https://t.co/FJa6TbkDMt pic.twitter.com/87g5NJITsz 
— Federal Reserve (@federalreserve) September 18, 2024 
By the end 2024, markets are expecting a total reduction of at least 100 basis points in the first rate cut cycle in over 4 years since 2020.
But whether the Fed goes for 25 or 50 bps, the biggest trigger for stock prices to move up or down would be Powell's motivation behind the cut.
Asset classes from stocks, currencies and fixed income could all log swings in the immediate aftermath of the Fed decision.
While easing US interest rates are directionally positive for equities in general, “we should keep in mind interest rates are just one variable in a complex adaptive system that determines the direction of Indian equity markets”, said Anoop Vijaykumar, Investments and Head of Research at Capitalmind.

 Your SIP corpus has grown. Should your investment strategy change too?
 As your SIP corpus grows from a few lakhs to Rs 1 crore, the risks change too. Here's when to reassess your investment strategy.
 Priyadarshini Maji 
 November 01, 2026 / 09:58 IST 
 --> 
 Representative Image: Grow your portfolio, shift focus from funds to asset allocation. 
 Grow your portfolio, shift focus from funds to asset allocation.
 Reassess your strategy when corpus hits 5x annual SIPs.
 Reduce equity exposure gradually as financial goals approach.
 Did our AI summary help? 
 Market Mastery
A 20 percent fall in a Rs 3 lakh mutual fund portfolio means a decline of Rs 60,000. But the same percentage fall on a Rs 1 crore portfolio translates into Rs 20 lakh.
The percentage decline is identical, but the amount at stake changes considerably.
 Also read: Multiple SIPs, same stocks? How to know if your mutual funds are actually diversified 
So, if your systematic investment plans (SIPs) have helped you build a sizeable corpus over the years, should you continue with the same funds and investment strategy?
The answer depends not just on how much your investments have grown, but also on your financial responsibilities and when you need the money.
"In the early years, your biggest asset is the monthly contribution, not the portfolio," says Aditya Agarwala, Chief Investment Officer and Co-Founder at Investvalue Capital.
When the corpus is relatively small, regular SIP contributions can help investors accumulate more units during market corrections. But as the corpus grows, market movements begin to have a much larger impact on its value.
Agarwala says the focus should gradually shift from simply selecting funds to managing asset allocation and concentration risk.
For instance, a substantial allocation to small-cap or thematic funds may have seemed reasonable when the portfolio was smaller. But as wealth grows, the same exposure could lead to significant fluctuations in the accumulated corpus.
 Also read: Gold, debt or REITs? How the top five multi-asset funds are investing your money 
Investors should also review portfolio overlap, expense ratios and potential losses during market corrections, rather than focusing only on returns.
 When should investors reassess their strategy? 
There is no fixed corpus threshold. Rs 50 lakh may represent a substantial part of one investor's savings but only a fraction of another's wealth.
Agarwala suggests reassessing the portfolio when its value reaches around five times the investor's annual SIP contributions, as market movements can start having a greater impact than fresh investments.
Life changes are equally important. Marriage, children, home loans, supporting ageing parents or approaching retirement can alter how much investment risk a person can afford.
The more important question is whether the investor's existing asset allocation still matches their financial goals.
 Should equity exposure reduce as goals approach? 
An investor saving for retirement 20 years away can generally afford more equity exposure than someone who needs Rs 30 lakh for a child's education in three years.
Agarwala suggests gradually reducing risk as financial goals approach.
 Also read: Silver prices have halved from record highs: Buy more, hold or reduce exposure? 
For goals more than seven years away, an equity-heavy allocation may be appropriate. Between five and seven years, investors can begin building debt exposure.
With three to five years remaining, he suggests considering equity exposure of around 50–60 percent in the goal-specific portfolio. During the final one to three years, most of the required amount can gradually move towards relatively lower-risk instruments, such as suitable short-duration debt or liquid funds.
These are illustrative guidelines, not fixed rules. The allocation should depend on the investor's circumstances and the goal's flexibility.
 How a suitable SIP portfolio can become risky 
Consider an investor who started SIPs at age 30 with Rs 25,000 a month and an aggressive 85 percent equity allocation.
Twelve years later, his corpus has grown to around Rs 1.3 crore. He now has a home loan, dependent parents and a child whose education could cost Rs 40 lakh in five years.
Yet his portfolio still holds nearly 90 percent in equities, with substantial mid- and small-cap exposure.
A 30 percent fall in the equity portion could reduce his portfolio's value by approximately Rs 35 lakh.
The original strategy may have been appropriate, but his financial circumstances have changed.
The sensible approach would be to gradually separate money needed for education from long-term retirement investments, rather than reducing equity exposure across the entire portfolio.
 Don't continue SIPs without reviewing the portfolio 
Even without changing funds, a portfolio's allocation can shift as markets move. Strong equity returns, for instance, may push equity exposure above the intended level.
Agarwala recommends reviewing the portfolio annually or when allocation drifts more than 10 percentage points from the target.

Rahul Ghose, Founder and CEO of Octanom Tech and Hedged, expects the IT sector to extend its rally further, as chart patterns suggest that the current uptrend is more than just a relief rally.
"On the monthly timeframe, Nifty IT has formed back-to-back bullish engulfing candles. That is a strong reversal signal after a long stretch of underperformance," he said in an interview with Moneycontrol.
With the IT index showing signs of strength, Ghose believes Coforge is a stock worth accumulating on every pullback. He also sees a similar chart structure in Tech Mahindra and recommends keeping the stock on investors' radar.
"Both are heading into all-time-high territory, where there is no overhead supply. That makes precise targets hard to set, but technically a 20–25 percent upside is possible over the medium term," he said.
 Do you expect the rally in the Nifty IT index to extend further from a technical perspective? 
Yes. The charts suggest this is more than a relief rally. On the monthly timeframe, Nifty IT has formed back-to-back bullish engulfing candles. That is a strong reversal signal after a long stretch of underperformance. On the weekly chart, an inverse head-and-shoulders pattern is taking shape. A decisive weekly close above its neckline would add a measured-move target to the structure. The momentum is already visible: the index reclaimed 32,500 on Friday, having gained about 17.7 percent over the past month.
After a near-18 percent move in a month, some consolidation would be healthy. I would use dips to accumulate rather than chase strength.
 Do you expect Nifty 50 to break out and sustain above 23,200? 
Yes. On the weekly chart, Nifty has formed a Morning Star at the 22,180 support, followed by a strong bullish candle, a classic reversal from a well-defended zone. Friday’s close of 23,053 was the first close above 23,000 in eight sessions. Short-term targets are 23,500–23,600, with 22,180 as the key support.
 Do you see a greater likelihood of crude oil prices moving lower rather than higher in the coming weeks? 
Yes, on a risk-reward basis. Crude may look bullish in the very short term, but it is approaching a major resistance zone of Rs 10,100–10,200 per barrel on MCX, followed by Rs 10,400. Prices have topped out around this zone multiple times. That kind of overhead supply rarely gets cleared without a fresh, sustained trigger. MCX November crude tested Rs 9,828 last week before settling near Rs 9,650.
At current levels, risk-reward does not favour fresh buyers, barring intraday trades. The more probable path over the coming weeks is a rejection from the resistance zone rather than a clean breakout.

With the IT index turning strong, this is a stock to accumulate on every pullback. Tech Mahindra has a similar chart structure and is worth tracking alongside. Both are heading into all-time-high territory, where there is no overhead supply. That makes precise targets hard to set, but technically a 20–25 percent upside is possible over the medium term.
The stock is taking support at a rising trendline after a strong set of numbers. The chart supports a move towards Rs 4,100–4,200.
 Do you see the possibility of a fresh leg of sharp upside in Apollo Hospitals? 
Yes, the setup is promising. On the monthly chart, Apollo has formed a classic hammer, with support at both a rising trendline and the monthly 20 EMA. When a long-term trendline and a key moving average converge at the same zone, it usually marks a high-quality support area. The stock gained 9.3 percent this week to close at Rs 8,448, its highest level of the week. The buying also appears to be genuine accumulation. Delivery volumes on October 28 were about 79 percent above the 5-day average.

 Several INDIA bloc leaders reiterated their demand for the CEC to step down while participating in the demonstration. (Screengrab of live stream | Rahul Gandhu/YouTube) 
 INDIA bloc held a mega rally at Delhi's Ramlila Maidan.
 Opposition demanded CEC Gyanesh Kumar's resignation.
 BJP organized a counter-march regarding 1984 riots.
 Did our AI summary help? 
 Market Mastery
The INDIA bloc on Sunday, November 1, organised a mega rally at Delhi's Ramlila Maidan, escalating its confrontation with Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in electoral rolls and the Election Commission's Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise.
Thousands of Opposition supporters gathered in the national capital for the 'Chalo Delhi' march, with senior leaders from several parties participating in the demonstration and demanding Kumar's resignation. The protest came a day after the INDIA bloc organised a symbolic public impeachment programme against the CEC at Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge's residence in New Delhi.
The Opposition has raised concerns over alleged large-scale voter deletions and demanded changes to the electoral process, including replacing Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs) with paper ballots.
 Rahul Gandhi accuses BJP of shutting shops in Connaught Place 
Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi accused the BJP of forcibly closing commercial establishments in Delhi's Connaught Place, alleging that the move had caused financial losses to traders ahead of the Opposition's demonstration.
In a post on X, Gandhi said participants had been encouraged to visit local markets and purchase goods while attending the march. However, he alleged that they found the shops shut when they arrived in Connaught Place.
"We told everyone that when you come here for the march and the mega rally, buy things, do some shopping. But, while coming to Connaught Place here, we found out that the BJP has forcibly shut down every single shop. So, you should know who is causing the loss to the traders, and how it's happening!" he said.
Earlier, Gandhi had shared the proposed route of the demonstration, asking people to join the procession from Connaught Place or gather directly at Ramlila Maidan.
"Delhi, get ready! Save the Vote, Save the Nation. Come to Connaught Place, let's march together. Or meet directly at Ramlila Maidan - but you must come. #ChaloDilli," he wrote.
 Opposition leaders seek Gyanesh Kumar's resignation 
Several INDIA bloc leaders reiterated their demand for the CEC to step down while participating in the demonstration.
Congress MP Syed Naseer Hussain said the gathering represented people from different parts of the country and indicated that similar programmes would be organised elsewhere.
"The massive surge of people you see here has risen from across the entire country. Similar programs are set to take place in every city throughout India," he said.
Himachal Pradesh Chief Minister Sukhvinder Singh Sukhu also called for Kumar's resignation, saying, "Gyanesh Kumar should resign."
Congress MP Manickam Tagore maintained that the Opposition's principal demand was the CEC's removal.
"The energy is full, and you are also seeing the 'Josh', and we want the resignation of Gyanesh Kumar. That is the only thing we are asking... everybody has to bow down before the people's power," he said.
Rajya Sabha MP Kapil Sibal described the demonstration as a significant political moment, declaring, "This is the beginning of the end of BJP".
Shiv Sena (UBT) MP Sanjay Raut also indicated that the Opposition was seeking a change in the political establishment.
"Kranti aa rahi. Revolution. Hum regime change ki taraf jaa rahe hain," he said.
Samajwadi Party MP Awadhesh Prasad said the demonstration was intended to defend democratic rights rather than target anyone.
"This rally is not intended to harm anyone; rather, it is aimed at saving democracy in this country—at protecting the right to vote, which was granted by Babasaheb Bhimrao Ambedkar. This will be a historic rally, and it will have far-reaching consequences," he said.
 Senior leaders join march to Ramlila Maidan 
The procession began at the Minto Road-Connaught Place junction and proceeded towards Ramlila Maidan amid heightened security arrangements.
Among those participating were Rahul Gandhi, Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge, Congress MP Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, National Conference leader Farooq Abdullah, Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav, NCP-SCP MP Supriya Sule, TMC chief Mamata Banerjee, TMC general secretary Abhishek Banerjee, RJD leader Tejashwi Yadav, Jharkhand Chief Minister Hemant Soren, Telangana Chief Minister Revanth Reddy, Jammu and Kashmir National Conference leaders, CPI leader D Raja and PDP chief Mehbooba Mufti.

 US Secretary of State Marco Rubio addresses Iran, Brazil, Pakistan-Afghanistan tensions and Quad cooperation at a press conference following the G20 Foreign Ministers' Meeting in Atlanta.
 Moneycontrol World Desk 
 October 31, 2026 / 23:05 IST 
 --> 
 US Secretary of State Marco Rubio 
 US prefers diplomacy with Iran but has military capability.
 Rubio highlighted Quad cooperation after the Atlanta meeting.
 US denied involvement in Flavio Bolsonaro leaving Brazil.
 Did our AI summary help? 
 Market Mastery
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Saturday said the United States has the military capability to achieve its objectives in Iran if President Donald Trump decides to take action, but stressed that Washington would rather resolve the situation through diplomatic channels.
Addressing a press conference in Atlanta at the conclusion of the G20 Foreign Ministers' Meeting, Rubio said Trump had not taken a decision on military action and that there was no announcement on the matter.
"The President's observation is that the United States remains the most highly capable military power on Earth. We can achieve military objectives if we choose to pursue them. He hasn't made a decision, and I have no announcement to make in that regard today," Rubio said.
He added that the administration was confident of its military capabilities but did not consider such action lightly. "If we needed to take military action, we would have the ability to do so. We have everything we need to be successful, but we would prefer to resolve this peacefully," he said.
According to Rubio, Trump's preference in dealing with international challenges was to pursue a diplomatic settlement wherever possible. He also said the US President did not consider engaging in negotiations or holding meetings with other leaders a concession.
"The President's preference in any challenge around the world is to try to solve it diplomatically and peacefully, if possible," Rubio said.
He added that Trump would have already acted militarily had that been his preferred approach, saying he could have taken such a step weeks or months earlier.
 Rubio accuses Iran of threatening regional security 
Rubio also criticised Iran over its conduct in the region, accusing Tehran of pursuing a confrontational approach towards neighbouring countries since the 1979 revolution.
"Iran has been waging war against its neighbors in the region since 1979," he said.
The US Secretary of State also pointed to threats against commercial shipping, describing them as a reminder of conflicts from earlier periods.
"We live in a world in which a country is openly saying, 'We will blow up commercial ships.' Think about that. This sounds like something from 100 years ago or 80 years ago," Rubio said.
He linked energy security to the broader economic consequences of regional instability, noting that fluctuations in energy costs have implications across the economy.
"Energy costs are embedded in the costs of everything we buy and everything we pay for, which is why the U.S.'s energy dominance and self-sustainability policies are so important," he said.
While reiterating Washington's preference for diplomacy, Rubio maintained that the US had the military resources required to meet its objectives should the President decide to pursue that course.
 US was not involved in Flavio Bolsonaro's departure from Brazil 
On Brazil, Rubio denied that the US government had facilitated the arrangements for Flavio Bolsonaro, an opposition leader, to leave the country and travel to the United States.
Asked about reports concerning Bolsonaro's departure following his loss to Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, Rubio said the US administration had not been involved in organising his travel.
"We were not involved in Flávio Bolsonaro's arrangements in terms of leaving Brazil. At least the U.S. government was not involved directly," he said.
In a clarification of earlier unconfirmed reports, Rubio said the US State Department had not facilitated Bolsonaro's travel.
"The State Department didn't facilitate anything," he said.
Rubio explained that Bolsonaro had previously held a US visa and that Trump had followed through on his earlier remarks that he would be permitted to enter the country.
The clarification came amid reports concerning the Brazilian opposition leader's travel to the US after his electoral defeat to Lula.
 Pakistan concerned over terrorism originating from Afghanistan 
Rubio also addressed tensions between Pakistan and Afghanistan, saying Islamabad was worried about terrorist attacks being carried out from Afghan territory.
According to the US Secretary of State, Pakistan believes the Taliban administration has not taken adequate measures to prevent such attacks and has consequently acted against the threat.
"Pakistan is concerned about terrorist attacks that are being sponsored from the territory of Afghanistan. They think that the Taliban has not done enough to constrain those attacks, and they've taken action against it," Rubio said.

docs.title: Stock recommendations for 2 November from MarketSmith India
docs.text:
Markets 
 Stock recommendations for 2 November from MarketSmith India
 MarketSmith India 12 min read 2 Nov 2026, 06:01 AM IST 
 Summary
 MarketSmith India reveals its top stock recommendations for today, 2 November. Get expert insights into the best-performing stocks to guide your investment decisions. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Stock market recap: Benchmark equity indices Sensex and Nifty rose for a second consecutive session on Friday, buoyed by strong buying in IT stocks and earnings-led gains in Trent, the Tata Group’s retail arm.
 The Sensex gained 308.49 points, or 0.42%, to close at 74,459.53, while Nifty 50 advanced 116.35 points, or 0.51%, to settle at 23,053.10.
 For the week, the Sensex rose 1.8% and the Nifty 50 2%. The recovery helped the Sensex finish October 2.7% higher, ending a two-month losing streak after declines of 5.8% in September and 1.5% in August. The Nifty rose 1.9% in October, after declining 6.1% in September and 1.2% in August.
 Foreign portfolio investors bought more than ₹ 14,000 crore of equities during the week, including primary-market investments. Domestic institutional investors bought another ₹ 7,062 crore. Indian equities found dual triggers this week as the country's largest IPO, Jio Platforms, delivered a strong debut, listing at 21.4% above its issue price. Meanwhile, the market found some solace as the US Federal Reserve held interest rates steady, though it maintained its caution on inflation.
 Two stock recommendations by MarketSmith India: 
 Buy: Coforge Ltd (current price: ₹ 2,045) 
 Why it’s recommended: Strong demand for AI-led engineering, cloud, and digital transformation services, backed by a record order book and large-deal wins across key verticals. Margin expansion and accelerated revenue growth driven by AI-enabled delivery capabilities and integration benefits from acquisitions such as Encora. 
 Key metrics: P/E: 41.39, 52-week high: ₹ 2,061.80, volume: ₹ 1,248.62 crore 
 Technical analysis: Cup base pattern breakout 
 Risk factors: Exposure to global IT spending cycles, where delays in client technology budgets can impact revenue growth and deal conversions. High dependence on North American and European enterprise demand, making earnings sensitive to macroeconomic slowdowns and currency fluctuations. 
 Buy: ₹ 2,025-2,055 
 Target price: ₹ 2,350 in two to three months 
 Stop loss: ₹ 1,930 
 Buy: Sai Life Sciences Ltd (current price: ₹ 1,557) 
 Why it’s recommended: Beneficiary of the global outsourcing trend and China-plus-one strategy, supported by its integrated CRDMO platform and deep relationships with leading global pharma companies. Capacity expansion into high-growth areas such as peptides, formulations, and late-stage commercial manufacturing provides a strong long-term growth runway.
 Key metrics: P/E: 86.40, 52-week high: ₹ 1,697.00, volume: ₹ 194.31 crore 
 Technical analysis: Reclaimed 50 DMA 
 Risk factors: Revenue visibility depends on the success and progression of clients’ drug-development pipelines, which are inherently uncertain. Regulatory compliance risks at manufacturing facilities and execution risks associated with large ongoing capacity-expansion projects. 
 Buy at: ₹ 1,541-1,565 
 Target price: ₹ 1,790 in two to three months 
 Stop loss: ₹ 1,470 
 How Nifty 50 performed

docs.title: Festive-season clean-up: how to declutter your mutual fund and stock portfolio
docs.text:
Mint Money 
 Festive-season clean-up: how to declutter your mutual fund and stock portfolio
 Jash Kriplani 5 min read 1 Nov 2026, 03:07 PM IST 
 Summary
 Too many funds and stocks can make investments harder to track and manage. Here’s how to weed out overlapping and underperforming holdings, rebalance your portfolio and keep your financial goals on track. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Alongside celebrations, India's festival season is also a time for clearing out cupboards, closets and homes. It may be a good time to turn your attention to something less visible but equally in need of a clean-up: your investment portfolio
 Over time, investments can accumulate across mutual funds and direct stocks, often with overlapping holdings or little contribution to overall returns. Keeping track of them, and assessing how each fits into the larger portfolio, can become an increasingly complicated exercise.
 A leaner portfolio makes it easier to monitor investments, assess performance and stay aligned with financial goals. Here is how to go about decluttering, starting with mutual funds and then moving to stocks.
 Decluttering your mutual fund portfolio 
 Start by putting together a complete list of your investments. Your consolidated account statement (CAS) provides a consolidated view in a single document. You can download it from registrars CAMS and KFin Technologies, or through MF Central.
 Next, revisit your asset allocation—the split between equity, debt and gold. “Check if a mutual fund investment has significantly distorted from your original asset allocation and therefore any trimming is needed there to re-balance the portfolio,” said Vishal Dhawan, founder of Plan Ahead Wealth Advisors
 “Eight-ten mutual fund schemes should be adequate for most investors, depending on their goals and timelines,” Nisreen Mamaji, founder, MoneyWorks Financial Services.
 A core-and-satellite structure can help keep the portfolio manageable. The core, comprising diversified equity or index funds, debt funds and gold, should be aligned with long- to medium-term goals. “You can keep a well-diversified core portfolio with funds that complement each other well and change only when a fund lags its category and benchmark for several quarters,” said Deepak Chhabria, chief executive officer and director at Axiom Financial Services.
 The satellite portion is where clutter can build up. Sectoral and thematic funds, new fund offers (NFOs) and last year's top performers can all find their way into a portfolio. Keep this allocation small and be selective about what stays.
 Schemes in the same category often hold the same stocks, especially in the large-cap category. A portfolio with too many equity funds “starts to resemble the broader market,” blunting its ability to outperform, said Ankur Punj, managing director and business head at Equirus Wealth. A Nifty 50 index fund can do that job at a lower cost.
 Most Indian equity funds follow a growth-oriented investment style. A value or contra fund can provide some balance. Fund-house concentration is another factor to consider. “If you have too many funds from the same fund house, consider trimming exposure there, to mitigate any impact on your portfolio if a fund manager quits or the fund house runs into a period of underperformance due to its investment philosophy,” Chhabria added.
 “Equity funds that make up less than 5% of the portfolio, and that you no longer add to, can also go. Even a strong run in it will barely move your overall returns,” said Amol Joshi, founder of Plan Rupee Investment Services.
 Decluttering your stock portfolio
 The same principle applies to direct equity holdings. Too many stocks can make it difficult to identify underperformers and assess what each holding contributes.
 “The more holdings you have, the harder it is to spot the laggards, and beyond a point the portfolio simply tracks the market,” Punj said.
 Start by getting a consolidated view of your holdings. These are available through your broker's app or website. If you have multiple demat accounts, you can download a consolidated account statement from the depositories—National Securities Depository Ltd or Central Depository Services (India) Ltd.
 Looking at direct holdings alongside mutual fund investments can also reveal overlaps that may otherwise go unnoticed. For instance, holding HDFC Bank and ICICI Bank shares as a large part of your direct stock portfolio, while also owning three large-cap funds, could leave you with substantial exposure to the banking sector. Banks carry significant weight in frontline benchmark indices, and large-cap funds typically have considerable exposure to the segment.
 Just like with mutual funds, it is important to keep track of your stock investments.
 “Check for stocks with less than 1% weights and sell them if they are not adding any value to the overall portfolio. Review the thesis you had in mind for each stock and see if it still holds good. If you don’t recollect the thesis or bought it on just a tip, then sell it regardless of its performance. Use the freed-up cash to invest in a sounder stock or mutual fund. Weakening of a company’s fundamentals could be another reason to sell a stock,” said Aarati Krishnan, head of advisory at PrimeInvestor Financial Research.
 Keep taxes in mind
 A portfolio clean-up should also account for the tax implications of selling investments. Capital gains taxes may apply, so the order and timing of sales matter.
 Prioritize selling loss-making investments first. If you end up booking some capital losses, it can be used later to offset capital gains and save on taxes. Remember, you can adjust short-term capital loss against both short term and long-term capital gains in any financial year. Long-term capital loss can be set off only against long-term gains.
 If you are looking to sell an underperforming mut

docs.title: Singapore once thrived on chokepoints—now they could strangle the free port
docs.text:
Opinion 
 Singapore once thrived on chokepoints—now they could strangle the free port
 David Fickling 4 min read 1 Nov 2026, 07:30 PM IST 
 Summary
 The city-state's wealth rests on a vulnerability—its much larger neighbours' control over vital chokepoints. With Indonesia cutting pipeline gas supply amid a change in the tone of international relations towards seeking leverage by exploiting dependencies, Singapore may be facing stormy seas ahead 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Stand on a clear day atop Singapore’s Marina Bay Sands hotel and you can see the city-state’s promise and peril in a single glance. 
 In the foreground, a flotilla of ships lies at anchor, a reminder of how Singapore grew rich servicing immense global trade squeezed through the chokepoint of its narrow strait. 
 On the horizon, you can just make out the coastline of Indonesia, a country with almost 50 times Singapore’s population and 2,500 times as much land. 
 Its proximity is a reminder of how dependent that prosperity remains on good relations with Singapore’s much larger neighbours. 
 Such issues are top of mind right now. For weeks, the view has been obscured by a haze drifting across the water from wildfires on Indonesian islands. Singapore passed laws a decade ago to combat this recurring public-health catastrophe, but has struggled to enforce them amid intransigence from its neighbour. 
 Just days after the city announced measures against 10 Indonesian companies over the blazes this month, Jakarta started cutting pipeline supplies of natural gas to Singapore. 
 The decision may have an innocent explanation. Singapore has shifted towards LNG and away from Malaysian and Indonesian piped energy in recent years, anticipating that its neighbours will use more of their own supplies as their economies expand. A key link allowing Indonesia to divert gas locally was completed just weeks ago, and the affected exports represent less than 2% of daily demand. 
 But recent comments from Jakarta’s energy distribution minister don’t inspire confidence. He warned neighbouring countries to “be careful” about annoying Indonesia if they don’t want their exports cut off. 
 The whole episode is another unpleasant reminder of the vulnerability underlying Singapore’s prosperity. For more than two centuries, it has thrived as a free port, in a world where chokepoints to trade have been progressively dismantled. 
 The city was established by the British to bypass the Dutch stronghold in Java, and its most important nation-building projects in the 1960s and 1970s repeated the model by making it a key node of emerging commercial networks, from oil refining, to container shipping, to long-haul aviation. 
 Throughout all that, however, Singapore has remained acutely aware of the chokeholds its larger neighbours control. Political separation from Malaysia in 1965 raised fears of water supplies being cut off. A costly programme of desalination, recycling, harvesting and reservoir-building would now allow near-self-sufficiency in a crisis. 
 The same can’t be said for energy. Even LNG supplies could be severed by a naval blockade. Nuclear power has been considered, but comes with its own challenges: You could fit almost the entire nation inside the 20km mandatory-evacuation zone. Plans underway to install 4GW of solar panels by 2035 could leave about 5% of the country under silicon and glass, and still meet barely a 10th of electricity demand. 
 Separate plans to develop renewable projects and transmission lines stretching to Vietnam, Laos, Cambodia, Malaysia, Indonesia and even Australia would at least diversify electricity suppliers. But those connections could, in theory, be cut off with the flick of a switch. Singapore’s driving role in establishing the power grid now taking shape across Asean can best be seen as an attempt to spread the risk across a web of mutual dependencies. 
 That’s the hopeful vision. In a world of multilateralism, peace and trade, small maritime republics can grow fabulously wealthy as nodes for global commerce and capital. Venice, an inspiration to Singapore’s founding generation, followed that model for centuries. 
 The worrying part is what came afterwards. As Europe’s commercial order gave way to an age of revolution, mass armies and nationalism, Venice’s wealth proved little protection against the larger powers surrounding it. 
 Napoleon extinguished the thousand-year republic in 1797 and it was traded back and forth like a bargaining chip between France and Austria for decades before being subsumed into the modern Italian state in 1866. 
 We could be entering a similar moment. The rising force in international relations is the chokepoint maximizer, looking for leverage over computer chips, critical minerals and trade flows to subdue its rivals. This year’s conflict over the Strait of Hormuz is a prime example. With barriers rising to commerce, migration and capital, free ports like Singapore are in lonely waters. 
 “If there were no international law and order, and big fish eat small fish and small fish eat shrimps, we wouldn’t exist,” founding father Lee Kuan Yew mused in 2007. 
 Lee’s successors must hope the great-power conflict brewing today is a passing storm, rather than a permanent shift in the global climate. ©Bloomberg

docs.title: Investing abroad via MFs: cap the investor, not the industry
docs.text:
Mint Money Investing abroad via MFs: cap the investor, not the industry Dhirendra Kumar (Value Research) 4 min read 1 Nov 2026, 06:00 AM IST Summary The privilege of overseas investment remains reserved for the wealthy. Small investors looking to invest abroad deserve a regulated, cheap way for doing so too. The answer: an individual cap per investor to make foreign investments Gift this article Check your portfolio This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you. Subscribe to enjoy similar stories. Subscribe now A few days ago, at an event in New Delhi, I asked Reserve Bank of India Governor Sanjay Malhotra about a strange situation for Indians who want to invest abroad, who have two main routes. One is Indian mutual funds that invest abroad. This route is simple because it works like any other mutual fund. You invest in rupees, can invest small amounts, run SIPs, and Sebi regulates it like domestic mutual funds. But this route has been largely blocked since 2022. All mutual funds together are limited to $7 billion in overseas investments, plus a separate $1 billion for foreign exchange-traded funds (ETFs). The RBI set this limit in April 2008, and it has not been raised since, despite the explosion in mutual fund investing. In 2008, the industry managed about ₹ 5 trillion. Today it manages more than ₹ 80 trillion. The second route is through GIFT City, the Gujarat International Finance Tec-City, an 886-acre enclave near Ahmedabad that counts as offshore for financial transactions. Under the Liberalized Remittance Scheme (LRS), any Indian can send up to $250,000 a year abroad, including into dollar-denominated funds that some asset management companies (AMCs) have launched in GIFT City. This route has its own regulator and isn't bound by the $7 billion ceiling. A few months ago, I wrote approvingly about it, and I still think a large investor should understand it. But it is not a route for someone who wants to start a ₹ 5,000 SIP. The minimum is usually $5,000, the all-in cost of some feeder funds is close to 3%, and anything above ₹ 10 lakh a year attracts a 20% TCS (tax collected at source), which blocks your money even if it’s eventually credited back. The business has gone there anyway. Fund houses have lined up to launch GIFT City funds for resident Indians: five opened by July, and more have since. The pooled cap did not stop money from leaving the country. It only decided who could take it out. Tighter leash on overseas investments? The governor said the RBI was monitoring investments through the GIFT City route. Then, disarmingly, he turned the question around and asked me what I thought should be done. Meanwhile, the stakes have gone up. A business television channel has carried a ‘source-based’ report that the RBI has suggested to the government that investment remittances under LRS, which need no approval today, should each need RBI approval. If something like this happened, and the governor said the RBI was watching GIFT City flows, practically every route for investing abroad would be shut. Here is my considered answer, thought through more thoroughly than a quick Q&A allows. The basic issue is that the well-regulated, cheaper, easier way to invest in the world is shut, while the costly, complex way that only the rich can use remains open. Cap the investor, not the industry First, the main route for investing abroad should work like any domestic mutual fund. If the worry is that money leaving the country must be watched, this is the cleaner solution, because every rupee goes through a Sebi-regulated fund house. And democratizing investing abroad means opening the mutual fund route, not rationing it to those with wealth to spare for an offshore account. Second, and most importantly, the limit should be per person and annual, not a single pooled limit for the entire country. A modest per-person annual cap, say $10,000, would let the RBI defend reserves without shutting out small investors because big investors got to the pooled limit first. $10,000 a year is enough for a monthly SIP of over ₹ 70,000, far more than most small investors need. It would also control what leaves the country each year, which is what matters for the rupee. The pooled limit is a blunt instrument. Once it is full, it shuts the door on everyone. A per-person limit may not have been practical in 2008, because tracking one investor’s foreign investing across fund houses would have been hard, if not impossible. Now, with PAN and Aadhaar linked to every investment account, that problem has gone. The industry’s registrars can already see each investor’s holdings across fund houses by PAN. Some global diversification is an important part of a mutual fund portfolio. So, that would be my answer to the governor: cap the investor, not the industry. A modest annual limit per person would serve the regulatory purpose while also giving investors who need it most an easy route. Opinion 
 India’s market slump: Here's why palliatives aren't enough to attract foreign investors
 Mint Editorial Board 3 min read 2 Nov 2026, 07:30 AM IST 
 Summary
 Changes in the capital gains tax alone won’t bring back foreign investors. Policymakers need to push through difficult reforms to drive the growth of high-value globally competitive firms. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Indian equities rank among the worst performing emerging market assets today, despite the rebound in October. The benchmark Nifty 50 index has fallen 12% this year (17% in dollar terms), Bloomberg data shows. 
 Among major emerging markets, only Indonesian equities have fared worse, with the benchmark IDX Composite index falling 42% this year (46% in dollar terms), following a warning from Morgan Stanley Capital International (MSCI) that Indonesia might lose its emerging market status. 
 The slump in Indian markets is partly because of large-scale selling by foreign portfolio investors (FPIs), who have pulled out about ₹ 3 trillion from Indian equity markets so far this year, a decadal high. The outflows have weakened the rupee, and in turn lowered the dollar returns foreign investors earn from Indian equities. 
 There are several contending explanations for the slump. One thesis points to the lack of artificial intelligence (AI) firms in the country. Since investors have poured gazillions of dollars into AI firms and AI-linked sectors, India has lost out. As the AI trade weakens, India would stand to gain, according to this thesis. 
 A second thesis emphasizes geopolitical tensions that have pushed up commodity prices. As a large commodity importer, India has been hit harder than the rest. Related to this, rising inflation and bond yields in the US have narrowed the spread between US and emerging market assets, weakening fund flows to emerging markets. 
 As geopolitical tensions subside and the global commodity cycle cools, India would be back in favour, the proponents of this thesis argue. 
 A third thesis emphasizes the lack of innovation among large Indian firms. Without the promise of sustained earnings growth, Indian stocks would remain unattractive to foreign investors, Bernstein Research analysts Venugopal Garre and Nikhil Arela wrote in a note to clients a few weeks ago. 
 If the AI trade weakens, or oil prices decline, foreign capital might return temporarily. But sustained flows would depend on “whether India can create new engines of competitiveness, innovation and global relevance,” they wrote.
 The new firms emerging in areas such as space, defence, semiconductors and deep-tech are currently too small to attract global capital at scale, the duo argued.
 None of these explanations suggest that changes in capital gains taxes can bring back foreign funds. To be sure, there are distortions in our capital tax structure, and this should be addressed, as this newspaper has argued earlier (see ‘ LTCG and STT: Optimize taxes that investors pay, ’ 19 October). Rationalizing capital gains taxes would help foreign and domestic investors choose more appropriate assets for themselves. But they are not a quick-fix to stem capital outflows. 
 The repricing of stocks in the current slump could itself rekindle interest in Indian markets. It is worth noting that foreign investors have invested heavily in initial public offerings in the recent past even as they have avoided overpriced stocks in the secondary market. 
 Policymakers should focus on difficult reforms that could catalyse the growth of high-value globally competitive firms in the country. These firms should be free to dedicate their resources to develop innovative products rather than expend them in managing the bureaucracy.

 About the Author

docs.title: PSUs are back—but they should exercise caution when implementing artificial intelligence
docs.text:
Opinion 
 PSUs are back—but they should exercise caution when implementing artificial intelligence
 Rajrishi Singhal 4 min read 1 Nov 2026, 08:00 PM IST 
 Summary
 Public sector units (PSUs) are having a rebirth globally, but their rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) has prompted an urgent need to install governance and regulatory guardrails. This is of special importance in India. Here's why. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Much like the circular nature of many fashion trends, there seems to be a renewed interest in reviving public sector units (PSUs). The levels of interest and intensity may vary from country-to-country but PSUs are definitely finding a second lease of life. 
 While economic exigencies—triggered by geopolitical flashpoints, broken supply chains, energy crisis, a climate emergency, tight money, heightened inflation and rising interest rates—may have necessitated a rebirth of PSUs globally, their rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) has prompted an urgent need to install governance and regulatory guardrails. This is of special importance in India. 
 The reason is that a PSU duality exists in India which aggravates the risks. The government’s public disavowal of PSUs exists cheek-by-jowl with heavy reliance on them. 
 While many ministers have publicly stated that PSUs drain national resources, official data demonstrates that the PSU comeback movie is playing out in India as well. 
 An annual survey of PSUs by the department of public enterprises—excluding banks, insurance companies and departmentally run companies—shows that the number of PSUs in India grew from 298 in March 2015 to 495 by March 2025, a 66% growth in 10 years. 
 Global data also shows a spike in PSU growth. According to the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), a Paris-based multilateral think tank, both the number of PSUs and the value of their assets in real terms have roughly doubled between 2013 and 2024. 
 This indicates the growing significance of PSUs, especially their expanding role in the global economy. An OECD report, Ownership and Governance of State-Owned Enterprises 2026 , further confirms the scale of PSU contribution to the global economy: 33,834 financial and non-financial PSUs had combined assets of $141 trillion in 2024, equivalent to 126% of global gross domestic product (GDP). 
 In terms of optics, the PSU resurgence may seem counter-intuitive when viewed against the Indian government’s recent disinvestment of majority shareholding in IDBI Bank in favour of Canada-based Fairfax Holdings. 
 While this disinvestment had been delayed for many years, its impending closure has now emboldened officials to announce a long list of assets for sale and monetization. At the same time, the government has both a monetary as well as strategic reliance on the public sector for achieving some of its targets. 
 The government is dependent on dividends from PSUs to meet a part of its non-tax revenue targets. Excluding surplus transfer from the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), the government received over ₹ 89,000 crore as dividend income from PSUs during 2025-26. 
 Even if we assume that RBI’s surplus transfer will remain unchanged during the current year ₹ 2.87 trillion, the government has budgeted to receive over ₹ 1.04 trillion as dividend income from PSUs during 2026-27. 
 But PSUs also have a larger strategic role. As oil companies, for example, they provide strategic price and supply stability during crises. Many manufacturing PSUs operate in sensitive areas where allowing private or foreign investment could end up endangering national security. 
 PSU banks, given their extensive network, provide the last-mile linkages for multiple government welfare schemes, including crediting direct benefit transfers to beneficiary accounts. In times of crisis, PSU banks act like conduits for liquidity or interest rate transmission. 
 Whenever RBI has to smoothen currency volatility, market trades are often coordinated through the foreign exchange desks of PSU banks. More importantly, funds for India’s defence imports are largely routed through PSU banks. 
 PSUs also meet another social objective by creating employment opportunities. In the public eye, Indian PSUs were always viewed as over-staffed and unproductive. 
 The truth is probably more nuanced. In terms of non-financial PSU employment as a percentage of total employment in the country, India does not figure among the top 20 countries in the OECD study. Surprisingly, Singapore tops the list with its PSUs having a 16% share in total employment. 
 This duality—publicized repudiation of PSUs while data reveals other truths—aligns well with India’s fuzzy PSU governance norms. The government has drafted clear and lucid guidelines for some issues but is vague on many critical areas. For example, there is a well-defined dividend policy framework for PSUs, but there seems to be no clarity on resolving the governance muddle inherent in PSU chairmen also acting as chief executives. 
 These grey areas may be advantageous when coercing PSU action or deploying moral suasion for strategic reasons. However, this same ambivalence could become a liability once multiple PSUs start implementing AI to improve productivity and efficiency standards. 
 The need for sharper and explicit regulatory guidelines has acquired some urgency, especially because the speed of implementation seems to have overtaken the need for caution and risk mitigation. 
 As a recent McKinsey article argued, PSUs are not private businesses and, hence, the risk of getting AI wrong through hasty implementation has multiple pitfalls. 
 The solution, therefore, is to have clear-cut controls put in place through transparent and well-reasoned guardrails and regulatory structures. 
 The author is a senior journalist and author of ‘Slip, Stitch and Stumble:

docs.title: A new graphic novel captures the spiralling nightmare of death row prisoners in India
docs.text:
Lounge 
 A new graphic novel captures the spiralling nightmare of death row prisoners in India
 Aditya Mani Jha 4 min read 1 Nov 2026, 03:30 PM IST 
 Summary
 Based on the work of The Square Circle Clinic, ‘The Donkey Rider’, a graphic novel by visual artist Rai, shows the psychological cruelty of prison life, especially for death-row prisoners whose fates are caught in a limbo 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 The opening pages of the graphic novel The Donkey Rider by visual artist Rai (Amrita Barua) aren’t narrated by either of the two main characters—Ghurbat, a prisoner on death row, and law student Huma, who is petitioning to stop Ghurbat’s execution. Instead, Rai makes a house lizard the narrator of these stage-setting, mostly black-and-white, pages (the house in question is the one Ghurbat once lived in). After a few surreal observations on the philosophical implications of an abandoned home, the lizard has a David Lynch-flavoured conversation with Ghurbat’s disembodied head.
 For what turns out to be a grounded, realistic, sobering read about the death penalty (and the structural inequities baked into India’s legal-political systems), this is a remarkably bold opening gambit. The lizard represents survival in the face of impossible odds, that indomitable little part of every organism that wants to keep on living; it’s why we use ‘lizard brain’ to describe instinctive, automatic, survival-driven modes of behaviour.
 The Donkey Rider is based on years of research conducted by The Square Circle Clinic (formerly known as Project 39A). The raw material being fictionalised are true stories of death row convicts, and the mitigation reports filed on their behalf by lawyers and law students. Mitigation reports are forensic and socio-legal documents that seek to capture the detailed circumstances leading up to a convict’s crime. These reports often become the basis of amnesty or mercy petitions, and that’s the narrative format that Rai adopts in parts of The Donkey Rider .
 The Ghurbat chapters tell us his harrowing life story—losing his father and then his grandmother, being hounded out of a neighbourhood for being Muslim, chased away from public spaces by bigoted policemen.
 Ghurbat also shows us the drudgery and the psychological cruelties of all prison life, but especially life on death row. It’s important to note that the book never tries to excuse Ghurbat’s crimes—all it seeks to do is present a holistic view, to give us as much information about the man as possible.
 The Huma chapters are intended as an urban-dwelling, English-speaking person’s perspective on Ghurbat’s plight—simplistic at first and then expanding with every prison visit, not to mention every snide comment about her work delivered by a friend or family member.
 Indeed, this contrast is reinforced by their respective fictional settings: Ghurbat grows up in the village of “Rukawa”, whereas Huma grows up in the nearby big city, “Pulse”. “Rukawa” sounds pretty close to “rukawat” (“delay” in Hindi/Urdu) and conveys a sense of perpetual waiting, the limbo in which economically backwards under-trial prisoners languish behind bars with no sign of a trial (In The Donkey Rider, one such prisoner loses his sanity for being trapped in the limbo).
 The Huma chapters and illustrations are well-lit, clean-cut studies in middle-class apathy; even the characters spouting nakedly aggressive lines (“Representing that dirty leech? That’s pure evil!”) have been drawn in a darkly funny way. They’re monstrous caricatures rather than literal monsters, characters in a black comedy and not a flat-out horror film.
 The horror-film aesthetics come with the Ghurbat chapters as he reminisces about his devastatingly sad childhood, recounts the deprivation and desperation that led him to commit a horrific crime. The morbid, and often supernatural, stories narrated by his fellow condemned men enter these chapters as well.
 Peak horror mode
 Rai is clearly a child of the 1990s, and influences from that era sometimes turn up in unexpected, eye-catching ways. For example, during her first meetings with death row convicts, Huma compares the long walks down stone corridors to the experience of playing Wolfenstein 3D, a popular 1990s video game set in a (fictional) Nazi prison. At a different point, Rai reproduces a prisoner’s legend about ‘The Well’, and it turns out to be a pastiche of the blockbuster prison-escape classics The Shawshank Redemption (1994) and the Clint Eastwood-starrer Escape from Alcatraz (1979).
 Rai piles on the horror effectively when she needs to. Obsessive cross-hatching and black-on-black shading effects bring out Ghurbat’s psychological horror (negative space is also utilised masterfully throughout the book).
 The peak of this psychological horror mode is page 107, where Rai draws a full-page, top-down illustration of The Well, the spiralling nightmare of a prison where Ghurbat is being held.
 October 2026 marks the birth centenary of the French thinker, Michel Foucault, and The Well has been crafted in the image of the “panopticon” (a circular prison featuring cells arranged around a central observation tower) described by him and by its original designer, philosopher Jeremy Bentham (1748-1832).
 Because of its subject material, The Donkey Rider is seldom an easy read. It is, however, a deeply rewarding work, thanks to Rai’s thoughtful distillation of The Square Circle Clinic’s research, and her robust, versatile illustrations that capture a wide range of emotions and scenarios. Read it to expand your understanding of our justice system—and the work all of us need to do in order to reform it.
 Aditya Mani Jha is a Delhi-based writer.
