docs.title: Credit card interest calculator: What will a ₹50,000 unpaid bill cost you over 12 months? Interest math explained
docs.text:
On the other hand, it is vital to acknowledge the fact that paying only the minimum amount due on such debt and credit card bills may seem like a comforting and convenient option for cardholders, especially those with a tight monthly budget. 
 Still, leaving a large chunk of the bill unpaid can make borrowing increasingly expensive and difficult to manage over time. This is because credit card interest rates are among the highest forms of debt, and the outstanding balance can grow very quickly into a substantial sum if dues are not paid for several months in a row and the credit card account is handled recklessly. 
 For example, consider a ₹ 50,000 credit card bill to understand how quickly this debt can accumulate. If an individual leaves such an amount unpaid for months, it can have serious financial consequences. This write-up is dedicated towards discussing the same in detail. 
 Now, to better understand the implications of keeping ₹ 50,000 unpaid on a credit card for 12 months (i.e., 1 year), let us assume that the credit card-issuing financial institution charges an interest rate of 3.5% per month, equivalent to 42% annually. For example, suppose the entire outstanding balance remains unpaid for 12 months, with interest compounded monthly. Then the eventual calculations will be as follows: 
 Note: The calculations discussed above are illustrative; they do not include applicable late fees, fines, and other charges that will be imposed on the cardholder, depending on the card type and issuing institution. They are presented to highlight the importance of managing credit card debt responsibly; final figures may vary depending on the credit card and the issuing financial institution. 
 This means a ₹ 50,000 unpaid bill can grow to approximately ₹ 80,153 in a year, including minimal GST charges on the interest. Hence, the additional costs can increase by more than 50% of the initial amount in just 12 months or so if credit card debt is not repaid responsibly. 
 This highlights the importance of vigilance and awareness among all credit card holders. To ensure that credit card use remains pleasant and meaningful for the cardholder, making on-time repayments is essential. 
 Furthermore, these are illustrative estimates based on monthly compounding, not an exact issuer statement. Actual charges depend on the card's terms, holder’s credit profile, repayment history , daily interest calculation, payments and applicable fees, along with a host of other factors. 
 Credit card debt comes with very high interest rates on the borrowed funds. It becomes very difficult to manage if the borrower falls into the habit of paying only the minimum due and tries to sustain it for months. 
 Following such a habit does not prevent interest from accumulating on the remaining balance. Moreover, new purchases may also attract finance charges because the interest-free period can be withdrawn. 
 That is why, cardholders should prioritise clearing their outstanding balances, avoid unnecessary purchases and pay the total amount due by the payment deadline. If repayment is difficult, they should explore a structured repayment plan and seek guidance from a certified financial advisor to address the challenging situation, rather than allowing debt to accumulate. 
The key takeaway, hence, is that a credit card should be a payment convenience tool for meeting unavoidable expenses such as medical expenses and unavoidable payments, not an easy-looking option for lavish expenses, nor a long-term borrowing tool.
 Responsible repayment, constructive credit card debt management planning and keeping interest costs under control can prevent a manageable bill from becoming a financial burden. 
 Disclaimer: The calculations are illustrative. Actual interest and charges may vary depending on the credit card issuer, interest rate, repayment history and applicable fees. Cardholders should check their credit card statements for the exact amount payable.

docs.title: Mint Explainer | Hope or heartbreak: what will COP31 deliver?
docs.text:
Explainer Mint Explainer | Hope or heartbreak: what will COP31 deliver? Sayantan Bera 3 min read 1 Nov 2026, 04:51 PM IST Summary Nearly 200 countries will gather in Türkiye amid mounting climate risks, with financing for vulnerable nations, the future of fossil fuels and the fading 1.5°C target set to dominate negotiations. Gift this article Check your portfolio This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you. Subscribe to enjoy similar stories. Subscribe now The United Nations (UN) annual climate summit opens next week amid energy turmoil, wars, soaring food prices and an intensifying El Niño. As nearly 200 countries gather in Antalya, Türkiye, climate finance, fossil fuels and the burden of global warming will dominate the agenda. Here’s what to expect. What is on the agenda? The 31st Conference of the Parties (COP31), scheduled for 9-20 November, will run on two tracks. The first is formal negotiations, presided over by Australia’s climate and energy minister, Chris Bowen. Key sticking points include $1.3 trillion in annual climate finance for developing countries, support to help vulnerable nations adapt to climate shocks and the future of fossil fuels. The second covers the host’s voluntary initiatives, from cleaner cities and waste reduction to healthier oceans and greater electrification . Its headline ambition is to raise electricity’s share of global energy supply to 35% by 2035, from 23% today. What is India’s position? India is expected to press for an equitable outcome, calling on developed countries to honour commitments on climate finance, adaptation support and technology transfer. At a UN event in October, India argued that climate action must respect countries’ differing circumstances and development needs. It also cautioned against unilateral trade measures such as the European Union’s carbon border tax, which raises costs for Indian steel and other exports. New Delhi is also expected to seek adaptation support for vulnerable communities and a just transition framework to protect livelihoods. It will cite its achievement of 50% non-fossil power capacity in 2025, five years ahead of target. India has also updated its climate pledges, or Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC), for 2031-35. These include a 47% reduction in gross domestic product (GDP) emissions intensity by 2035 from 2005 levels and a 60% share for non-fossil sources in installed power capacity. What did the last summit achieve? COP30 , held in Belém, Brazil, in November 2025, produced a compromise deal. Countries agreed to work towards tripling adaptation finance by 2035 and reaffirmed the goal of mobilizing $1.3 trillion in annual climate finance by then. The deal also established a just transition mechanism to protect workers as economies decarbonize. But it sidestepped fossil fuels, offering no roadmap to move away from them. Brazil’s presidency said it would pursue voluntary roadmaps on fossil fuels and deforestation instead. Is the Paris climate goal already out of reach? The chance of limiting global warming to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels, as envisaged by the 2015 Paris Agreement, has been lost, according to the UN’s Emissions Gap Report 2026, released on 21 October. Warming is expected to breach that threshold and peak at 1.7-1.8°C around mid-century. Still, a return to the 1.5°C pathway by 2100 remains possible, though it would require cutting emissions by about 18% by 2030, 45% by 2035 and 69% by 2040 from 2025 levels, and removing roughly 320 billion tonnes of CO2 this century. Together, these offer a 50% chance of returning to the pathway. The report also notes progress: renewable energy has surged since the Paris Agreement, coal and oil supply have grown more slowly than projected, and climate policies have curbed emissions in many countries. Will COP31 reckon with the ‘super’ El Niño? COP31 opens as an unprecedented El Niño builds in the Pacific. The event is expected to make 2027 warmer than 2024, potentially setting a new record. El Niño is a natural climate cycle that compounds human-driven global warming but does not alter its long-term trajectory. It could, however, offer delegates a preview of a hotter world, with more severe droughts, floods and wildfires across regions. A late-October update from the University of Chicago’s climate impact lab projects 857,000 global deaths from El Niño-related extreme heat between June 2026 and March 2027. Gift this article Check your portfolio About the Author Sayantan Bera Sayantan is a National Editor at Mint. As a part of its Long Story team, he writes on food and nutrition, agriculture, rural economy and climate change. His work is a blend of ground reportage and analysis where he unpacks news and trends from India’s hinterlands.

He also co-authors a fortnightly newsletter ‘Climate Change and You’ with a belief that how different sectors of the economy, and we as a species, shape and are shaped by the unfolding climate crisis, is a defining story of our times.

Before joining Mint in 2014, Sayantan worked as a correspondent and photographer with Down to Earth, an environment fortnightly, covering eastern Indian states. There he wrote on mining, environment, forests, tribes and farming. He’s been a journalist for 17+ years, most of it at Mint where he learnt how to tell human interest stories dispassionately.

Before joining journalism, Sayantan worked as a researcher at multiple think-tanks and at a non-profit, specializing in rural development and finance. Sayantan holds a Master’s and M.Phil. in Economics from Jawaharlal Nehru University, New Delhi.

docs.title: Why India’s bridges are under troubled waters

Long Story 
 Why India’s bridges are under troubled waters
 Neha Bhatt 10 min read 1 Nov 2026, 05:21 PM IST 
 Summary
 Bridges, tunnels and highways are crucial lifelines for connectivity and commerce. Yet, many suffer failures during or after construction, taking a heavy toll on lives and wiping out massive investments. In this deep dive, Mint looks at why things go wrong and how they can be fixed. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 New Delhi: The cracks began to appear within weeks. In mid-July, the 63-kilometre, six-lane Kanpur-Lucknow expressway, built at a cost of ₹ 4,200 crore, had opened with much fanfare. Inaugurated by a glittering cast of political leaders, including Uttar Pradesh chief minister Yogi Adityanath and road transport and highways minister Nitin Gadkari, it was expected to cut travel time between the two cities from 2-3 hours to 30-40 minutes.
 By early August though, dozens of potholes pockmarked the expressway, forcing The National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) to partially close it for repairs. For commuters, the promise of a seamless drive across vast fields quickly faded as the highway turned into a makeshift repair site.
 Industrial fans lined the route to dry the wet, crumbling road, and excavators and roadrollers worked to patch damaged portions, pushing traffic onto diversions and stopping heavy vehicles from using the highway altogether.
 Similarly, in July, the ₹ 16-crore approach road near Dehradun’s Nanda Ki Chowki bridge caved in just 16 days after its inauguration. A month earlier, a ₹ 26-crore railway road overbridge in Buxar suffered partial structural failure and came apart days after opening.
 Last July, the Gambhira Bridge in Vadodara district collapsed, sending vehicles into the Mahi river, killing 22 people and severing a vital transport link. That tragedy came less than three years after a 19th century suspension bridge in Morbi, also in Gujarat, collapsed barely five days after it was opened during the Diwali season. The footbridge, touted by the state’s tourism department as an “artistic and technological marvel”, had been opened after six months of renovation by a private company. Around 140 people were killed, 55 of them children, and many more were injured when it came apart on 30 October 2022.
 Bridges, tunnels, highways and key public infrastructure have long stood as symbols of the country’s culture, history, and engineering prowess, becoming crucial lifelines for connectivity and commerce.
 In recent years, many such projects have been inaugurated, including the Chenab Rail Bridge in Jammu and Kashmir, the world’s highest railway arch bridge; the Sela Tunnel in Tawang, Arunachal Pradesh, located at an altitude of over 13,000 feet; Mumbai’s Atal Setu, India’s longest sea bridge; and the New Pamban Bridge in Tamil Nadu, the country’s first vertical-lift railway sea bridge. And yet, many of India’s infrastructure projects frequently suffer failures during or after construction, sometimes taking a heavy toll in lives.
 The list of infrastructural failures is long. According to government figures, a total of 72 projects have either collapsed or shown major deficiencies on national highway stretches from 2020 to 2025. Media reports suggest the figure is far higher—over 170 bridge and flyover failures between 2021 and 2025.
 So, why do these disasters occur, and why do they occur so frequently?
 No longer about nation building
 According to urban researcher Aravind Unni, construction quality, as well as the nature and scale of disasters, have changed, with a direct impact on urban modern infrastructure. “In the past, infrastructure was built to last—designed to withstand almost anything. The projects we built, like dams, were built with a 100-year perspective. They were more than just mega-projects; they were about nation-building,” he says.
 The emphasis on delivering projects in compressed timelines can often come at the cost of quality.
 In the case of the Kanpur-Lucknow expressway, for instance, a team of experts from Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Kharagpur engaged by the NHAI reportedly found that the highly plastic soil, which is fine-grained silt used as the foundation underneath the thick upper layers, was the likely cause of the cracks. It was found to be weak, lost structural strength when wet, and shifted under heavy loads. Plastic soil is usually stabilized with chemicals to reduce its moisture sensitivity.
 Added to this was an inadequate drainage system, and unpaved shoulders of the expressway meant for further expansion, which allowed water to accumulate and become trapped beneath the pavement, further destabilizing the base. Currently, repairs are being carried out on about 80 patches on the expressway.
 According to the findings of the state government’s probe into the incident, the Gambhira bridge collapse was caused by structural failure—systemic corrosion over time and a crushing of the pedestal and articulation joints that support the deck of the bridge on which vehicles ply. These critical support points connecting separate sections of the bridge disintegrated under vehicular pressure, decay, and structural fatigue.
 A special investigation team looking into the Morbi collapse blamed it on severe structural corrosion, shoddy repair work, and extreme overcrowding. Nearly half of the wires of one of the two main cables of the suspension bridge were corroded, it found. Old suspenders were welded with new ones, and the walking structure was made up of rigid aluminium panels instead of flexible wooden planks.
 Systemic issue
 According to construction, engineering and infrastructure consultant Devanshu Pandit, while India has undertaken a massive amount of infrastructural projects, it does not yet have the capacity to match the demand.
 “We are missing sufficient equipment and manpower. Contractors are movin

docs.title: Companies have a solution for the skilled trade shortage: more women
docs.text:
Global 
 Companies have a solution for the skilled trade shortage: more women
 Te-Ping Chen , The Wall Street Journal 5 min read 2 Nov 2026, 06:42 AM IST 
 Summary
 As women make inroads in male-dominated fields, firms look to improve jobsite culture. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Sammy Cossairt has tried call center work, waiting tables and hoisting concrete. She prefers hoisting concrete.
 The 36-year-old tower crane operator in Nashville, Tenn., who works 12-hour shifts, helps lift and move rebar and buckets of concrete from a perch often hundreds of feet in the air. This isn’t what she envisioned when she received a liberal arts associate degree more than a decade ago, but after nearly a decade on the job, she feels at home in her crane.
 “I’m out in the sun, making my mark on the world,” said Cossairt, who makes $120,000 a year. “I think more women would love to get in and make men’s money doing this work, if they only knew.”
 The skilled trades have long been a boy’s club. But more women are breaking in, drawn by well-paying jobs that are in high demand. To keep them coming, many companies are courting women like Cossairt through new benefits and perks, including paid maternity leave and more flexibility. They are also trying to create a more welcoming work environment while cracking down on off-color jokes and catcalls on male-dominated jobsites.
 The federal government tracks female participation in fields such as construction, and installation and repair, which includes jobs such as plumbers, carpenters and auto technicians. As of last year, women made up about 4.4% of those workers. But they have made mostly steady gains, with that figure rising from 2.9% a decade earlier.
 At Universal Technical Institute’s campus in Exton, Pa., career services director Katie Yurick said women are enrolling partly because the industry has grown more tech-infused. Automotive technicians can hook up cars to computers for diagnosis, and plenty of in-demand jobs—such as welding and electrical work—can trade as much on brains and attention to detail as brawn.
 “These jobs aren’t even dirty jobs anymore,” said Yurick, adding that she has also heard from employers who say they are trying to hire women, believing they possess high maturity levels and are detail-oriented.
 UTI’s student body, which spans 17 campuses across the U.S., is now 8% female, quadruple what it was five years ago. In some areas, such as collision repair and auto refinishing, that figure is even higher, at 19%.
 “Our industry needs this workforce,” said Maja Ericksen, executive vice president at construction company Mortenson, which in 2024 began offering 12 weeks of paid leave for birth mothers in its skilled workforce. More than 10% of Mortenson’s skilled workforce is now female, up from 7% a decade ago.
 “There aren’t too many careers you feel are AI-proof, and being in the skilled trades is one that isn’t going away,” Ericksen said.
 Women have broadly outperformed men in the labor market in recent years. This partly reflects booming growth in fields that traditionally employ more women, such as healthcare and social assistance, while women also are making inroads in traditionally male-dominated jobs.
 Kym Gardner, 39, a project engineer in Charlotte, N.C., said that as a child, she never thought about working in the field. Her mother was a teacher, her father a computer analyst. “No one really talked about it, it wasn’t considered to be a career,” she said. “The expectation was to go to college.”
 But in high school, she grew interested in architecture, found a construction mentorship program and quickly fell in love with seeing buildings rise from the ground up. Now the mother of three children, including a 5-month-old, starts her days on site and works remotely in the afternoons—flexibility she said helps give her peace of mind and ensures she doesn’t have to sacrifice her caregiving duties.
 Her company, Turner Construction, is growing fast and needs all the workers it can get, said president Abrar Sheriff. The company hit $29 billion in revenue last year and expects around $35 billion this year, fueled in part by work on data centers. More worker flexibility, including creature comforts such as heated and cooled bathrooms with running water on worksites, or regularly cleaned breakrooms, are part of the pitch.
 “We need more people to come into our industry,” Sheriff said.
 Elsewhere, construction company Skanska has taken steps such as ensuring female employees have correctly sized gloves, helmets and work boots, rather than forcing them to make do with male-sized gear. Deila Ray, who spent a decade as a pipe welder and now teaches the trade in high school, said she had to shrink her own gloves with fire when she started in the industry.
 Skanska this year also started mandating inclusivity for all its team leaders, encouraging them to be more aware of different workers’ needs, said Ayesha Adams, who joined Skanska in 2023 as its inaugural director of culture and engagement.
 “You can get people all day, but how do you keep them here?” Adams said.
 Some states are trying to make work in the trades more accommodating for women. Both Washington and Illinois, for example, have in the last few years passed laws requiring nursing rooms for mothers on construction sites, as well as refrigerators to store breast milk, flexible break schedules and access to water for cleaning.
 Construction companies are also tackling another issue: workplace harassment. At Turner, senior leaders there get on a call within four hours of any incident being reported. In one recent case in Texas, a subcontractor’s entire project crew of around a dozen men were replaced when that company couldn’t identify who had written derogatory graffiti about female employees, said Sheriff, Turner’s president.

docs.title: EPFO Foundation Day Quiz 2026: Full list of winners to be awarded today | What is EPF, EPS, PMVBRY, Vishwas 2026 scheme
docs.text:
The quiz was conducted from 13 to 23 October 2026 and drew 8,584 participants from across India. It aimed to create awareness regarding EPFO's schemes and services, including the Employees’ Provident Fund Scheme, 2026, the Employees’ Pension Scheme, 2026, PMVBRY and Vishwas 2026. In a blog post, MyGov announced that all participants would receive e-certificates and added, "EPFO and MyGov extend their appreciation to all participants for their enthusiastic participation and look forward to their continued engagement in future MyGov activities." The quiz focused on four EPFO schemes and initiatives aimed at supporting employees and employers. Here’s a closer look at each. According to an official release, the new EPF 2026 scheme, launched under the Code on Social Security, 2020, replaced the erstwhile Employees' Provident Fund Scheme. The EPF 2026 scheme enables members to build their retirement savings through contributions and accrued interest. It also permits members to make partial withdrawals from their savings for specified purposes, including housing, higher education, marriage, and medical treatment, subject to prescribed conditions. The erstwhile Employees' Pension Scheme , 1995, was replaced by the new EPS 2026 under the Code. EPS 2026 provides monthly pension benefits to eligible members on superannuation, retirement, or disability. Further, it gives pension benefits to eligible dependants of deceased members, including spouses, children, and other eligible family members. The Pradhan Mantri Viksit Bharat Rojgar Yojana ( PMVBRY ) encourages formal employment by offering incentives to eligible first-time employees and employers creating additional jobs. According to a release, PMVBRY "reinforces the national priority by encouraging first-time employment and supporting job creation. Through a transparent, Employees' Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO)- administered framework, it strengthens workforce formalisation while creating opportunities for both employees and employers." Announced in August 2025 with a budget of ₹ 99,446 crore, the scheme covers two years from 1 August 2025 to 31 July 2027. It aims to create jobs for over 3.5 crore people, including 1.92 crore first-time employees, by encouraging young workers to register with EPFO and join the organised sector. In terms of incentives, PMVBRY offers the following: a. First-time employees earning up to ₹ 1 lakh a month can receive a one-time payment equal to one month’s EPF wage, subject to a maximum of ₹ 15,000. The amount is released in two instalments, the first after six months of service and the second after 12 months of continuous employment and completion of a financial literacy programme. b. The scheme also offers benefits to employers, who can receive up to ₹ 3,000 a month for two years for each eligible additional employee earning up to ₹ 1 lakh a month and retained for at least six months. It is a one-time settlement scheme for employers, launched by EPFO to resolve eligible disputes over damages or penalties for delayed provident fund contributions. It aims to reduce litigation and encourage employers to regularise compliance. It covers four categories of cases: - Cases where orders for penalties or damages are under challenge before a judicial forum; - Final damages or penalty orders where recovery is pending or has been only partly made, including Recovery Certificate (RRC) cases; - Cases where notices have been issued but final orders for damages or penalties are yet to be passed; and - Cases where notices for penalties or damages are yet to be issued. docs.title: Lula's re-election: Brazil’s public finances are already precarious—is the country on the path to a crash landing?
docs.text:
Opinion 
 Lula's re-election: Brazil’s public finances are already precarious—is the country on the path to a crash landing?
 Gene Frieda 4 min read 1 Nov 2026, 07:00 PM IST 
 Summary
 The President's spending plans could drive up inflation, hurt the currency, push up real interest rates and thus weaken economic growth. Under such conditions, the country will be unable to gain any lift, no matter how hard it flaps its wings. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Brazil has an unfortunate habit of disappointing. Despite the country’s exceptional natural-resource endowment, its growth trajectory resembles what Brazilians call the flight of a chicken ( voo de galinha ): a brief flutter followed by an inevitable fall back down to Earth. President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s surprise re-election raises the risk of another letdown. 
 By the time he leaves office in 2030, Lula will have occupied the presidency for 16 (non-consecutive) years. Today, Brazil’s public finances are already precarious, following nearly four years of loose fiscal policy. Public-sector debt has risen from 73.8% of gross domestic product (GDP) in 2023 to a projected 86.6% by the end of 2026. 
 Stabilizing debt at this level would require a sustained primary fiscal surplus of at least 1.5% of GDP. Instead, Brazil is expected to run a primary deficit of around 0.5% of GDP this year. 
 The government’s fiscal targets exclude some expenditure that contributes to borrowing requirements. Adjusting for the economic cycle and temporary fiscal measures, the International Monetary Fund puts Brazil’s structural primary deficit at an estimated 1.3% of potential GDP in 2026. 
 Without fiscal adjustment, Brazil’s debt could increase by another 10 percentage points over the next four years. But there is no sign Lula will pursue the necessary changes. In the final weeks of the campaign, he promised additional benefits, subsidies, and tax relief that local estimates suggest could cost 0.4-0.6% of GDP in 2027. Some measures can be implemented without new legislation, but their continued financing will require parliamentary agreement. 
 With the government’s “expenditure ceiling” already fully allocated, new spending requires offsetting cuts, additional revenues, or further exceptions to its fiscal framework. None will be easy. Congress, with more than 20 parties represented, has expanded its influence over budget allocations in recent years. Legislators have strong incentives to defend existing benefits and spend any additional resources. 
 Furthermore, at 32.4% of GDP, Brazil’s tax burden is already unusually high for an emerging economy. Congress has repeatedly resisted the government’s revenue-raising efforts over the past two years, and the newly elected legislature is substantially more right wing. 
 Lula faces a choice between adjusting fiscal policy proactively or waiting for financial markets to force his hand. The political incentive to delay is considerable. Former president Dilma Rousseff’s attempt at fiscal tightening following her 2014 re-election alienated parts of her political base and failed to prevent her impeachment in 2016. 
 Lula may prefer to let market pressure provide the political justification for unpopular measures. But markets have an incentive to test that reluctance, raising borrowing costs and potentially forcing a more painful adjustment later. 
 The new Congress will also test Brazilian institutions. Over the next four years, Lula can nominate replacements for four of the Supreme Court’s 11 justices and fill all nine seats on the central bank’s governing board. These appointments all require Senate confirmation. 
 Historically, this has been little more than a formality, but the Senate’s rejection of Lula’s Supreme Court nominee, Jorge Messias, in April—the first such rejection since 1894—suggests that the days of rubber-stamp confirmations may be over. 
 Both institutions will be subject to intensifying political tensions. The Supreme Court will adjudicate disagreements over executive authority, congressional spending powers and constitutionally protected expenditure. The central bank will face pressure to accommodate a fiscal position that the political system appears unwilling to correct. 
 This pressure is already evident. The central bank’s Lula-appointed governor, Gabriel Galípolo, frustrated elements of the ruling party by resisting faster interest-rate cuts before the election. Lula now has an opportunity to reshape the bank’s leadership. 
 Yet financial markets have moved in the opposite direction: following Lula’s victory, interest-rate futures began pricing renewed tightening, rather than the cuts expected before the election. The conflict between political demands for lower rates and market demands for tighter policy could become a major test of the bank’s independence. 
 Inflation has exceeded the upper bound of the central bank’s target range for nearly two-thirds of the months since it was granted operational independence in 2021. Deteriorating fiscal credibility could raise inflation expectations and real interest rates, while weakening the currency. 
 The resulting pressure on the banking system is also growing, with non-performing loans already rising. Further monetary tightening could aggravate credit losses and constrain lending. 
 Brazil’s floating exchange rate, substantial foreign-exchange reserves and strong commodity exports, together with the fact that its debt is denominated predominantly in its own currency, reduce its exposure to a balance-of-payments crisis. But these do not eliminate the domestic costs of fiscal deterioration. 
 As investors demand higher compensation for inflation and fiscal risks, borrowing costs will rise, worsening debt dynamics. Persistently high real interest rates depress private investment and weaken growth. 
 Political polarization makes consensus

 Tech Mahindra prioritises growth blitz after margin boom
 Jas Bardia 8 min read 1 Nov 2026, 12:22 PM IST 
 Summary
 As he completes 12 quarters at the helm next month, Tech Mahindra CEO Mohit Joshi talks about prioritizing organic growth, decoupling headcount from revenue in the AI era, and eyeing larger acquisitions next year. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 This December, Mohit Joshi will complete three years—or 12 quarters—as chief executive of Tech Mahindra Ltd, the country’s fifth-largest tech services firm. Over this period, the company has expanded in roughly nine quarters while nearly tripling its profitability, a record few peers can match. Though Tech Mahindra expects margin expansion to continue beyond the next fiscal year, driving immediate growth remains its chief priority. 
 In a virtual interview with Mint , Joshi discusses his strategy for the AI era along with his hits and misses as CEO. Edited excerpts : 
 As you complete three years as CEO, how has the journey been, and what are some of the hits and misses?
 I think it’s been challenging, but rewarding. The challenge was to accomplish growth and margin improvement in a period when the industry itself has been growing very slowly. Earlier, we used to get a discount to our price-to-earnings ratio compared to our larger peers; now we get a premium. With AI, we have to continue building the differentiated AI for each of our service lines. So that is a work in progress. I think the financial services growth for us has been a little bit slower than what I expected. We have opened a couple of fairly large logos, so I feel very optimistic about the road ahead. 
 Is AI leveling the playing field between mid-cap and large-cap IT firms, given that mid-caps have posted faster growth in recent years?
 I don't see anything structural that gives mid-caps a long-term growth advantage. Clearly, large-cap players may have more application maintenance and more long-term contracts. So there is, you know, the upfront challenge of AI productivity . (But) I don't feel it is a foregone conclusion that the largest players will lose or the smaller players lose because even among the mid-caps, there has been a fairly significant divergence in growth between them.
 What is your North Star for Tech Mahindra? Do you want to grow at the rate of mid-caps or scale revenue and become a larger IT services firm?
 The focus will very much be on growth gaps. Also, most of our growth has been organic, right? See, if you look at the mid-caps, a lot of the growth has been inorganic. I think we have maybe 10 or 20 basis points of inorganic growth. Everything else is completely organic. So we want to focus on organic growth, and we want to make sure that we are among the fastest-growing players in the industry. Over time, I feel we will also start looking at inorganic again and how we can acquire capabilities in areas where we may be relatively small. We really don't want to acquire just to pick up revenue, because that is a disaster. Our priority will be growth and some level of margin expansion that goes along with it. 
 When will you start looking at inorganic then?
 If we have to change our capital allocation policy, and maybe keep a little bit more for inorganic growth, we will look at the change when we announce the next phase of the plan, I would guess, anytime after April 2027. But for now, the focus will very much be on organic with maybe some small tap-in acquisitions. But beyond that, beyond March 2027, I suspect that we will start looking much more keenly at larger acquisitions. 
 Are you betting on data centres, or are you thinking of picking up stakes in AI companies? If not, if Project Indus is your moat for growth going forward, are you pitching it as part of your deal constructs? How much revenue have you actually earned through the Indus offerings that you have?
 As far as data centres are concerned, I don't think that we want to. As for Indus, it started more as a research and development effort. It was an effort to prove that a system integrator out of India could build a large language model from scratch. 
 But at the end of the day, our total investment in Indus was a fraction, like a rounding error, compared to what it would take to build a large language model in the West. But that capability itself is very important because when we go to clients and we say we understand AI, that is sort of backed up by the fact that we have built a large language model from scratch. 
 The actual monetisation of Indus in terms of us selling Indus as a software has been very, very small, because while we had some discussions with people about loading Indus onto, let's say, laptops, that has not been a material source of revenue. 
 In two to three years, will headcount grow at a similar rate as your revenue?
 The relationship between revenue growth and headcount will not disappear, but it will weaken. And we are already seeing this start because if you build and deploy a pool of forward-deployed engineers in the region, that would give you significant revenue acceleration, maybe without significant headcount addition. As we move more and more to the higher value-added services, we'll get higher margins from that. You'll be able to deliver your business as usual with lower-headcount projects, and so you will get greater revenue productivity from that. 
 Since 2022, when OpenAI launched ChatGPT, has AI lived up to its hype? What's been your biggest learning about what AI will do in the coming years?
 I think AI has certainly lived up to the hype in terms of the increased maturity that we see from the models, the increased use cases and functionality, the multi-modal nature of the models, the fact that you can now see the thinking behind the model in plain sight, and the fact that it has moved from being only a generative AI architecture to now

 Why Indian tennis players are struggling to make the big league
 Deepti Patwardhan 5 min read 1 Nov 2026, 08:00 AM IST 
 Summary
 Without solid funding or structured support, India’s tennis players are left to navigate the relentless pro circuit alone, balancing high travel costs against shrinking odds 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 The walls of the airy cafeteria at the Maharashtra State Lawn Tennis Association (MSLTA) complex are adorned with pictures of the main show courts of the four Grand Slams: Australian Open, French Open, Wimbledon and the US Open. The courts that the cafeteria’s picture windows overlook are a world apart.
 As players toil in the wilting heat at the World Tennis M25 Mumbai event, which was held from 19-25 October, there are no stands, no spectators and no ball kids either as players have to chase down the yellow fuzzy orbs themselves. It is bare-bones tennis stripped of all its glamour and grandeur. It smells of sweat and survival.
 “Everyone here is either losing money or just breaking even,” says Indian player Sidharth Rawat, who has been on the pro tennis tour for around 15 years, working on a breakthrough to the big league.
 The in-between—that’s where the majority of Indian players seem to be currently.
 According to the latest rankings, there are no Indian singles players in the top-200, either in the men’s or women’s charts. Sumit Nagal, 29, is the highest-ranked Indian men’s player at World No. 269, followed by the 18-year-old Manas Dhamne at 391. On the women’s tour, Vaishnavi Adkar is the top-ranked player at 334 and Sahaja Yamalapalli (369) is the only other Indian in the top-400.
 The last time an Indian player competed in singles at a Grand Slam main draw was Nagal at the 2025 Australian Open. Nagal is also the last from the country to win a match at a major—the first-round clash against Alexander Bublik at the 2024 Australian Open. The last Indian to win a Grand Slam title was Rohan Bopanna, who captured the 2024 Australian Open men’s doubles title with Australia’s Matthew Ebden.
 Indian tennis was provided another reality check at the 2026 Asian Games, which took place from 19 September-4 October. For the first time since 1986, India returned without a single medal in the sport.
 Regardless of the level of competition, an Asian Games medal carries weight in Indian sports circles, opens the door to financial rewards from states and strengthens claims for accolades like the Arjuna Award.
 “For the players who are here (at Mumbai M25), I don’t think it makes a big difference,” says veteran Indian coach M. Balachandran, of the Asian Games disappointment. “They started with nothing, and they still have nothing. But where it may hurt Indian tennis is getting funding. They will look at the results and say, ‘Why should we put money when there are no medals to show?’ Programmes like TOPS (sports ministry-run Target Olympic Podium Scheme) look at results in multi-discipline events like the Asian Games, and if they see no benefit, they might not want to continue.”
 Support—financial, technical and tactical—has been the biggest missing piece for Indian tennis. As the sport has moved away from being an amateur pursuit to a cut-throat global profession, finding the right resources at the right time has become critical.
 National federations across the world are churning out players through structured programmes rooted in scientific training, while Indian players are largely left to fend for themselves.
 Barring a few private endeavours, such as academies set up by like Bopanna in Bengaluru and Somdev Devvarman in Chennai, and funding through CSR initiatives, there is little concerted effort to build a strong, sustainable tennis ecosystem.
 The Missing System
 “The gap between India and other countries keeps growing,” says Balachandran, who heads the Rohan Bopanna Tennis Academy (RBTA) coaching team, and works with some of India’s top players such as Adkar and Dhakshineswar Suresh.
 “Your game is only one aspect of it. How to use your game for a particular situation against that opponent in given conditions is the key to winning matches. From 17-20 is the most crucial age for tennis players, as they make that transition into the pro tour,” says Balachandran.
 “They need the right inputs, like training and tactical awareness to make the jump, at this critical time. “Unfortunately, most Indians don’t have access to that. They travel alone, without coaches and trainers, keep making the same mistakes. The later you breakthrough, the harder it gets because you keep losing money and confidence,” he says.
 Tennis is structured in a way that players have to play tournaments to earn money and ranking points. India does not have enough lower-grade tournaments to help them build a base, which means they have to travel abroad, at least around Asia, if not Europe and the US, to play a full tour schedule, which is about 20-25 weeks. That means they have to pay and arrange their travel, accommodation and food, with no guarantee on the returns. Indian legend Vijay Amritraj calls it “the highest-risk business you can be in”.
 There are over a thousand players each ranked on the ATP (men’s) and WTA (women’s) charts, and plenty more enter the fray each year. “You make money only if you are in the top 250,” says Rawat, who achieved his highest ranking of 430 in 2019. “For every tournament I play, I spend an average of ₹ 50,000,” adds Rawat. “That means to play a full tour, and travel just by myself, I need about ₹ 10 lakh every year.”

 Japanese investors deepen India bets, creating a bigger business opportunity for law firms
 Sneha Shah , Devina Sengupta 4 min read 2 Nov 2026, 05:59 AM IST 
 Summary
 Sifting sands of geopolitics has meant that India and Japan come closer. Last year, Japan pledged a target of JPY 10 trillion in private and public investments into India over the next decade. Since Aug 2025, 120 MoUs have been signed targeting over ₹ 1 trillion of cross border investments

 MUMBAI: Japanese money is flowing into India, and the lawyers who handle M&A, PE and venture deals are feeling the surge. Japan desks at leading Indian law firms report their busiest stretch in recent memory, with some adding lawyers and others racing to capture a bigger share of a growing fee pool.
 The momentum shows in a run of investments and partnerships announced over the past 12-18 months. MUFG Bank acquired a 20% stake in Shriram Finance, launched a dedicated venture capital fund for Indian start-ups and signed a strategic partnership with State Bank of India. Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation took a 20% stake in YES Bank, and Mizuho Securities plans to acquire a controlling stake in Avendus Capital. The Development Bank of Japan invested in HDFC Capital’s H-DREAM Fund.
 "Due to the increasing deal flow between India and Japan, across M&A and venture and PE investments, our lawyers covering the India-Japan corridor are finding themselves the busiest in the last 12-18 months,'' said Abhishek Guha, partner, corporate practice, at Trilegal. ``We are eyeing an increased volume of M&A and PE-related activity in this corridor going forward and are gearing up for a busy time ahead."
 The growing engagement comes amid shifting global geopolitics, the Russia-Ukraine war and rising US tariffs, which have brought India and Japan closer. Japan was among India's largest sources of foreign direct investment (FDI) equity inflows in the first half of 2026, investing $6.26 billion during January-June, according to government data.
"The India-Japan investment corridor is witnessing remarkable momentum, driven by global economic realignment, changing supply-chain strategies and India's strong growth prospects," said Rudra Kumar Pandey, partner and head of Japan desk at Shardul Amarchand Mangaldas & Co.
 Last year, Japan pledged 10 trillion yen (around $65-100 billion) in public and private investments in India over the next decade. Since August 2025, 120 memorandums of understanding (MoUs) targeting more than ₹ 1 lakh crore in cross-border investments have been signed, government data shows.
 India attractive destination 
 With Japanese companies reassessing their exposure to China amid rising competitive and profitability pressures, India is emerging as an attractive destination for long-term expansion. Against projected global growth of approximately 3.1%, emerging-market growth of around 3.7% and relatively modest growth across major advanced economies, India's growth trajectory stands out, Pandey said.
 India's expanding network of free trade agreements also offers Japanese businesses opportunities to collaborate with Indian companies, establish manufacturing operations and use the country as an export hub.
 "We are witnessing growing interest from Japanese corporations, financial institutions, private capital investors and, increasingly, small and medium enterprises. I expect this diversification to sustain strong momentum in cross-border M&A, joint ventures and investment activity over the coming decade," Pandey added.
 Japanese venture capital (VC) firms and institutional investors are also increasingly shifting their focus from Southeast Asia to India, drawn by stronger IPO momentum, rising exit opportunities and a more vibrant technology start-up ecosystem, Mint reported earlier.
 BeyondNext Ventures, Enrission India Capital, Incubate Fund Asia and Genesia Ventures are among the Japanese VC firms exploring India more aggressively as investments in their home market and Southeast Asia have failed to deliver significant exits.
 More business 
 The growing activity has translated into more business for law firms advising Japanese clients. Firms are responding by forging partnerships with Japanese law firms and hiring lawyers to handle the potential increase in work.
 In September, Argus Partners hired an entire team led by Saurav Kumar from CMS IndusLaw. Kumar joined as senior partner in the firm's corporate and M&A practice and head of its Japan and South Korea desk.
 "The nature of engagements in this corridor has broadened considerably, with significant deal activity emerging in green investments, critical manufacturing and new-age technology sectors. As transactions in these specialized domains were historically uncommon in the Indian market, they introduce intricate regulatory, legal and operational complexities that demand an exceptionally high calibre of legal expertise," said Kumar.
 On the private capital side, the pace of activity has also picked up. Around half a dozen deals and investment announcements have emerged over the past 12-18 months, including the transactions and partnerships involving MUFG, SMBC, Mizuho and DBJ.
 "These are not small stakes or small deals. They are large, complex acquisitions involving significant investments by Japanese financial institutions. This reflects growing confidence in their understanding of India's legal and regulatory environment, and a deep conviction in the country's growth story," said Rishabh Shroff, partner, co-head of private client and head of international business development at Cyril Amarchand Mangaldas.
 Such transactions require expertise in complex financial-sector M&A, backed by capabilities across tax, intellectual property and regulatory practice areas, he said.

docs.title: Serbia’s Gen Z students toppled a strongman. now comes the hard part.

Global 
 Serbia’s Gen Z students toppled a strongman. now comes the hard part.
 Georgi Kantchev , The Wall Street Journal 7 min read 2 Nov 2026, 06:51 AM IST 
 Summary
 Their electoral victory is a test for whether youth protest movements can build governments that work. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 BELGRADE, Serbia—Serbia’s Gen Z student movement pulled off what the country’s opposition parties couldn’t in 14 years: ousting one of Europe’s most entrenched populist and authoritarian leaders.
 But after sweeping last month’s parliamentary election, with around 53% of the vote, and ending Aleksandar Vučić’s grip on power, now comes the hard part. Can a movement built to resist power govern?
 “When you solve a problem, another three show up,” said cultural-studies graduate student Tara Blagojević walking across Belgrade’s Slavija Square, a focal point of protests against Vučić. “We solved one problem. Now we have other problems.”
 The students won’t take a single seat in parliament. Instead, they have handpicked an unlikely cast of mostly political outsiders to represent them, including a cardiologist, a former central-bank governor, a basketball legend and an opera singer.
 Joining them are dozens of academics more accustomed to lecture halls than the corridors of power. Most have never held political office.
 The student movement has yet to choose a prime minister, much less assemble a cabinet or even decide how it can influence the lawmakers it propelled into office. It must also find a way to keep united its politically diverse bloc, which includes nationalists, liberals and leftists.
 “What we lack in experience, we will make up for in integrity,” said Katarina Šćepanović, a high-school English teacher elected on the student slate. “We are figuring things out as we go along.”
 Serbia’s Gen Z-led political upheaval matters far beyond the Balkans. It tests whether youth movements can turn protest into electoral victory and then build governments that work.
 Across Europe, tens of thousands joined Gen Z-led protests in Germany on Saturday, while student demonstrations in France have grown into a broader movement over education and living costs.
 Elsewhere, youth-led uprisings in recent years have shaken political establishments, fueled by anger over corruption, deep distrust of political elites and the organizing power of social media. In Bangladesh, students helped topple a prime minister , only for an established party to win the subsequent election. In Nepal, a newer party swept to power after Gen Z protests. In Madagascar, the military took over following a revolt.
 The Serbian student movement can bring positive change for the country but “will face enormous challenges, including meeting their electorate’s expectations, maintaining the movement’s cohesion and forming a government while maintaining their collective approach as far as possible,” said Michael Davenport, former European Union and U.K. ambassador to Serbia. “They will be tested on all fronts.”
 The upheaval offers Serbia, a Balkan nation of some 6.5 million long pulled between the EU and Russia, a chance to rebuild its democratic institutions and revive its stalled ambitions to join the EU.
 But the victory doesn’t necessarily herald a geopolitical realignment. The students have opposed sanctions against Moscow, citing Serbia’s dependence on Russian gas and memories of sanctions against their own country in the 1990s. The movement also maintains that Kosovo, which declared independence in 2008, remains part of Serbia.
 Student-backed candidates have proposed an eventual referendum on Serbia’s EU membership, though it isn’t part of the movement’s formal election platform. Blagojević said the new government would put EU democratic standards into practice.
 The students hadn’t initially set out to take power. They wanted answers about a tragic incident.
 On Nov. 1, 2024, a canopy collapsed at the newly renovated train station in Serbia’s second city of Novi Sad, killing 16 people. For many Serbians, it became a symbol of alleged corruption and a state that had failed to protect its citizens.
 Students demanded investigations and accountability, occupied universities and organized silent vigils across the country. A mass rally centered on Belgrade’s Slavija Square in March 2025 drew hundreds of thousands in one of the largest protests in modern Serbian history.
 The anger ran deeper than the train station incident. Vučić’s Serbian Progressive Party had governed since 2012, while he dominated politics as prime minister and then president. Critics have accused his administration of pressuring the judiciary and controlling much of the media. His government has denied the accusations, portraying the protests as a threat to stability. Representatives of his party didn’t respond to a request for comment for this article.
 Dejan Šoškić, a former central-bank governor on the student-backed slate, described being vilified by pro-government media for criticizing economic policy. He said the protests were about making institutions work again, not simply replacing one set of politicians with another.
 “This is not the time for classical politics,” he said at the University of Belgrade’s economics faculty as students streamed through the halls toward morning lectures. “Classical politics comes once you re-establish the normal and proper functioning of the country.”
 For Blagojević, political protest runs in the family. She recalled that her grandmother protested as a dentistry student in 1968 and her aunt, an architecture student, took part in demonstrations in the 1990s.
 Blagojević joined students organizing through plenums , open assemblies at university faculties where participants debated and voted. Representatives chosen by those assemblies coordinated protests, media strategy and eventually the election campaign through

Opinion 
 Manu Joseph: How India's labour has made London a kinder city
 Manu Joseph 5 min read 1 Nov 2026, 06:30 PM IST 
 Summary
 India’s training of its poor to never feel empowered enough, to always know “their place,” and to never take seriously democracy’s biggest humbug, that all are equal, makes them good workers in jobs that the locals in the UK don’t want to do. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Part of our dying heritage is the dance of two Indian strangers as they approach each other on the street of an advanced economy. They avert their gaze, lower their heads, veer a little, as though to escape being bound by the same origin story. It is a ritual of sophistication, and it had its heydays when the chances were high that two Indians on such a street were from the upper class. 
 Now something has changed, at least in London. There are so many Indians in any given hour that they ignore each other, or they just gape because most of them are poor or lower-middle-class migrants. They are here to do work that English people had said they would do themselves after driving away Europeans in the name of Brexit. 
 The growth of the transient low-wage worker in London, led by Indians, has been extraordinary. Even two years ago, they were not this common. As a result, they have altered the public face of most of London. They have made it far less intimidating, and more amiable , informal and compassionate. This happens to a city when its visible workers don’t have the swag of equality. 
 Not long ago, the typical cafe in London was run by locals, or East European migrants whose tolerance for alien mannerisms and the misdemeanours of customers was low. In the superstore, when the attendant was speaking to a customer, you did not interject. 
 The waiter carrying a tray filled with plates could not be stopped to be asked a question. When the barista’s back was towards you, making coffee, they could not hear you. Everywhere, workers did only one thing at a time. Once, a street-side vendor was making a pancake, and an Indian made an order, as Indians do. The vendor raised his arms: “I only have two hands.” 
 London was particularly intimidating for Indians and other Asians who are accustomed to servility from people who do menial jobs. Just because a board said, “Please wait to be seated,” must they be rebuked for grabbing a table? 
 All that has gone, in most of London. Now it is poor migrants from poor countries who work at these places. When someone is passing an instruction to the kitchen, you can ask them a question about choices of milk, and they will not vibrate in disorientation. A worker in a superstore who is rushing somewhere can be interrupted with a question. 
 Indians have also transformed the public character of London in an odd way. Now the support staff speaks English. Twenty years ago, you could not be assured of getting by in Central London using English if you needed assistance, say, in the tube stations. Physically, London is too beautiful, too clean , too orderly, and its government too humane, to be an Indian city. But inside many buildings it feels like India. 
 India’s training of its poor to never feel empowered enough, to always know “your place,” and to never take seriously democracy’s biggest humbug, that all are equal, makes them good workers in jobs that the locals in the UK don’t want to do. 
 Migrants have also changed British homes. Britain’s upper middle class is beginning to resemble ours. They are pampered by cheap help. Chauffeurs are not common for them, but nannies are not rare anymore. 
 The money is good for the migrants. The UK is the new Gulf for many Indians, including Malayalee nurses who are in demand. 
 But most migrants I spoke to are not entirely happy. London is fearfully expensive, so they don’t exactly have a first-world quality of life. They live in small rooms, too many of them in that space, and far away from where they work. 
 An odd thing about people is that the quality of life of a city, all its beauty and clean air, is not as important as what they are familiar with and how a city makes them feel. India’s unsightliness, chaos and visible poverty make them feel less poor than in a spectacular city like London. 
 They have the intense sense of inferiority of being at the bottom of the society that they don’t feel in the sprawling poverty of India where there are millions below them. 
 Also, often what separates the happiness of a whole span of youth is the lottery of a good boss. Some migrants who said they were happy were those who said their employers were decent people and fair. But they were very few. 
 About 20 years ago, most of the migrant Indians who worked in London would claim they were students. They did come on student visas but chiefly to work. I continue to find such ‘students,’ but many of the migrants today come on proper work visas meant for them. There is a growing political acceptance in the UK that they need migrants for menial jobs, as the locals won’t do them. 
 The locals don’t love this entirely. They need the migrants but they may wish they were invisible, just as we expect the people who serve us to not come into conflict with the aesthetics of our beautiful homes. 
 One morning, I was in a Pret A Manger, watching an Englishman who was on the phone saying, “London is finished, it has gone to the dogs.” He was triggered by an impoverished woman of colour, probably homeless, who decided to sit across his table. 
 The waitress came to clear; the woman asked her to take away the croissant, which was not hers. He looked horrified even as he muttered more about the “end of London.” He turned to the next table for support but only found me there.

 The week ahead in numbers: Auto sales, PMI numbers, US mid-term elections
 Anjishnu Das , Payal Bhattacharya 5 min read 1 Nov 2026, 07:00 AM IST 
 Summary
 A look at the key economic developments, data releases and market events that could shape the week ahead. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Every week, Mint’s Plain Facts tracks key economic trends, data releases and global events shaping the week ahead. This week, domestic auto sales and manufacturing PMI figures will offer crucial signals on consumer sentiment and industrial momentum as India heads into the festive peak.
 Quarterly earnings from consumer staples majors will show how rising food inflation and a widening rural-urban price gap are affecting household budgets. In the US, mid-term elections will determine control of Congress and shape the legislative agenda in Washington.
 The Bharat Renewable Energy Summit, meanwhile, will bring into focus India's estimated $220 billion investment requirement to expand its clean energy infrastructure.
 Vrooming ahead
 After robust sales in September, the domestic automobile industry is heading into a high-stakes festival season, with Diwali approaching. October data from the Federation of Automobile Dealers Associations (Fada), expected this week, will offer an early indication of consumer demand during the crucial buying period.
 September saw vehicle sales across segments surge 31.8% year-on-year, led by major automakers such as Maruti Suzuki, Mahindra & Mahindra and Tata Motors. However, the growth was partly amplified by base effects, as purchases had been deferred ahead of a cut in the goods and services tax (GST).
 October will provide the first cleaner year-on-year comparison. Fada surveys point to strong dealer optimism, with more than 75% expecting sales growth to continue through the end of the year. Yet affordability remains a concern amid rising prices. Provisional sales data for the Navratri period, from 11-20 October, showed a 6.5% year-on-year sales decline.
 Business activity
 The final October Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI), due on 2 November, will offer a fuller picture of manufacturing demand, export orders and hiring as businesses prepare for the December quarter.
 Manufacturing faces a more uneven outlook, with slower purchasing activity and cautious hiring contrasting with stronger order inflows. Services, meanwhile, will be assessed on their ability to sustain growth amid domestic and overseas demand.
 Flash estimates released last week showed the composite PMI rising to 56.7 in October from 55.9 in September, its highest reading in four months. New export orders expanded at their fastest pace in six months, but employment growth was at its weakest over the period. Manufacturing PMI eased to 54.9 from 55.1, while services PMI strengthened to 56.2 from 55.2
 The flash survey also noted that input-cost inflation eased for a seventh consecutive month to a near one-year low in October, although higher transportation and steel costs continued to pressure businesses. Manufacturers sharply increased finished-goods inventories even as purchasing activity slowed.
 The final readings, alongside new orders, employment and selling-price trends, will be important for gauging business conditions heading into the December quarter.
 Rural squeeze
 September-quarter results from ITC Ltd and Marico Ltd on Monday will offer clues to the resilience of rural demand and consumer goods companies' ability to sustain volume growth as household costs rise. Both companies are constituents of the Nifty Rural Index, making their performance a useful indicator of consumption trends in rural markets.
 Rural inflation rose to 6.08% in September, its highest since June 2024, amid a deficient monsoon, strengthening El Niño conditions and an unfavourable base effect. The rural-urban inflation gap also widened to a 20-month high. This matters for FMCG companies as rural consumption accounts for 55.4% of the CPI basket, against 44.6% for urban consumption.
 Nomura expects food and beverage inflation to rise to 8.5-9% in October-November from 5.7% in August, raising the risk of weaker consumption after the festive season. In its 1 October report, the brokerage also flagged the convergence of rural volume growth with urban levels.
 Investors will watch volume growth in ITC’s cigarette and non-cigarette businesses and Marico’s Parachute and Saffola portfolios, alongside management commentary on pricing, margins and rural demand in the second half of fiscal year 2027 (FY27).
 Mid-term mandate 
 Americans will vote in the mid-term election on 3 November, in a contest widely viewed as a referendum on President Donald Trump's performance and that of his party. Voters will elect all 435 members of the House of Representatives and 35 of the Senate's 100 members. Republicans currently hold majorities in both chambers.
 Trump's approval rating has fallen to 37% from 52% in January 2025. A Pew survey found that the economy and inflation are among voters' top concerns, with 65% saying his policies had worsened economic conditions. Halfway through Trump's second term, the election offers voters an opportunity to hold his administration accountable and could determine which party controls Congress and the legislative agenda.
 However, the outcome is unlikely to drastically alter India-US ties or core trade and immigration issues. Trump’s presidential veto powers mean that even if the Democrats seize a majority in the House and Senate, they would be limited in impacting foreign policy, including stalled trade talks with India or the war against Iran that has sparked a global energy crisis.
 Green goals

 Arpita Akhanda reconstructs memories in her first major solo art show
 Avantika Bhuyan 5 min read 1 Nov 2026, 03:30 PM IST 
 Summary
 In her first major solo, multidisciplinary artist Arpita Akhanda looks at the body as a witness and an archive 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 For Arpita Akhanda, memory is not a distant concept. It is a living entity that continues to inform her present. The 34-year-old artist, based in Santiniketan, looks at her body as a memory collector. It carries experiences that extend beyond the physical form into other kinds of archives such as photographs, and textiles preserved by her family. Akhanda’s practice is rooted in the histories of her grandparents and three districts—Comilla, Barishal, Faridpur—now in Bangladesh. Following the Partition of Bengal, both sides of the family crossed the newly-constituted border and eventually settled in Odisha. She does not look at Partition as a standalone historical event, but delves into the constant aftermath as it permeates the ordinary rhythms of the family, passing down through generations.
 This idea of the body as a witness and archive runs like a thread in her first major solo, Under the Moon Across Many Waters , on view at Emami Art, Kolkata. Developed over two years, Akhanda has expanded her practice to look at paper weaving, photography, performance, drawing, kinetic installation and a fresh engagement with jacquard weaving. Born in Cuttack, bedtime for Akhanda meant listening to stories about how her family had left their village in East Bengal with just a brass vessel for water. Over time, the artist observed during conversations with her family that the same memories would often resurface in different forms, each time carrying a new note or emotional weight. She translates that repetition in her practice with the same archival images often recurring across different pieces in varied contexts.
 For her, the phrase “history repeats itself” holds immense significance. The act of repetition then becomes more than a decorative element. It becomes a conscious tool to observe, question, and understand the past in the present. “But repetition is also an act of erasure. Each new layer builds upon what came before while concealing parts of it,” elaborates Akhanda. “Something is preserved, and something disappears. This tension between familiarity and unfamiliarity, preservation and erasure, is something I continue to explore in my work.”
 Addressing gaps in the archive
 She works with the reconstructed image, be it in performance, video or kinetic installations. For instance, in the paper weavings, archival photographs are spliced, cut and then rewoven to create a fragmented image. In the Jacquard works, figures resemble tableau-like compositions suspended between “portraiture, historical reconstruction, and fiction, populated by people remembered, documented, and imagined”. The past and the present coexist and intersect.
 Reconstruction also gives her a chance to address the gaps and biases within archives. For instance, she became increasingly aware of how gendered family archives could be. Her paternal grandfather, who studied art at Santiniketan—a tradition Akhanda took forward—had access to a camera and meticulously documented his life through photographs, diary entries, and poems. His archive left behind physical traces through which his granddaughter could connect people, places, and events. Her paternal grandmother’s archive, however, existed differently. It lived in oral histories, textiles, and conversations during overnight stays. Her memories were transmitted through stories, gestures, and acts of making rather than through a formally documented record. This difference made Akhanda question what constitutes an archive and whose ways of remembering are recognized as historical evidence.
 Only recently did she learn more about her maternal grandfather’s history and his displacement from East Bengal during Partition. This discovery also made her reflect on how histories can remain unknown within a family for generations. Sometimes, information is not passed on because family members are unaware of it; at other times there may be a reluctance to revisit painful experiences, or silence itself may become a form of defence. For Akhanda, the act of retelling is not simply about filling a gap, but about looking into why it exists in the first place. “It emerges from a personal need to understand these absences and piece together fragments. I am not trying to arrive at a complete or definitive version of the past, but to understand how memories survive, what gets carried forward, and what remains invisible across generations,” explains Akhanda.
 This understanding of the archive as something living informs the work, Carry, Borrow and Sow, which is on view as part of the exhibition. She thinks of carrying, borrowing and sowing as ways in which memories travel, transform and take root in new places. “The archive is not static; it continues to live through the body, through objects, and through the ways we carry our past into the present and pass it on to the future,” she adds. Though the scope of her practice has increased, the choice of the medium stems organically from the kind of memory she is working with. She begins by collecting archival materials and placing them alongside institutional archives to understand how historical events have shaped personal histories.
 Akhanda organizes these materials chronologically and gathers as many associated physical traces as possible. When traces are missing, she turns to staged photography to reconstruct or narrate them. Photography lets her revisit an image while weaving allows her to fragment and reconstruct it, bringing together what remains and what is missing. docs.text:
Opinion 
 India's IT industry: What a 14th century scholar's ideas can tell us about it
 Nitin Pai 4 min read 1 Nov 2026, 06:00 PM IST 
 Summary
 Although he wrote about civilizations and empires, not technology companies, his observations about how societies rise and fall are useful in understanding what lifecycle stage tech giants are at and, more importantly, what they might have to do to continue to thrive. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Watching India’s information technology (IT) services companies discuss the extent of what they call “AI revenue deflation” in recent weeks, I was reminded of Ibn Khaldun, the 14th century North African scholar. 
 He wrote about civilizations and empires, not technology companies, but the outline of his observations are useful in understanding where our tech giants are and, more importantly, what they might have to do to continue to thrive. 
 Khaldun argued that societies rise and fall in cycles. Founders triumph over adversity and create a political institution. They are followed by builders who carry forward the growth. Next come the inheritors who rest on their laurels, and are finally succeeded by those who preside over loss and disintegration. 
 Like the Chinese proverb that gave wealth three generations, Khaldun framed the life of a state in four phases. The founding generations succeed in the desert because they are held together by a force of solidarity that he calls Asabiyya , which weakens amid the luxuries of the city and the injustices in an enlarged empire. 
 The decline happens when expenditure exceeds income and mercenaries fill the ranks. The empire is then overthrown by a new group with stronger asabiyya . 
 Now there are instances of dynasties and empires around the world lasting much longer than four generations, so Khaldun’s cycle is not destiny . 
 It does, however, other things for us. It tells us that the leaders and the circumstances they face are different at different times, and things that worked for the previous senior management team might not work for the current one. 
 We are alerted to how asabiyya —solidarity, coherence and a sense of common purpose—might be weakening amid growth, luxury, careerism and internal competition. 
 Companies more than empires find their options shrinking when margins get tighter, increasing the chances of mistakes and bad decisions. Finally, someone faster, nimbler and younger eats your lunch. 
 It is not an exaggeration to claim that the first generation of the Indian IT services industry were heroic: starting up in the licence-permit raj and then convincing a sceptical world of India’s technological and professional capabilities is nothing but that. 
 Not just founders but industry figures like the late Dewang Mehta were champions and cheerleaders who persuaded global investors and enterprises to put their money in India in the 1990s. That was a time when it was not clear whether India would persist with economic reforms, manage the proxy war in Jammu and Kashmir and navigate out of economic sanctions following the nuclear rests. 
 Sure, Y2K, business process outsourcing and the rest rescued us, but only because industry leaders sold the India story to the world. Contrary what some people might now believe, the global IT business didn’t fall on the laps of software engineers chilling out in Bengaluru’s parks. 
 I do not know which Khaldun phase our IT services companies are in today but I do not see any senior industry figure make bold declarations of how Indian industry is best placed to capture the global market for artificial intelligence (AI) adoption. 
 It is understandable that CEOs must account for slower revenue growth amid rising AI-related work, but such a conservative managerial approach completely ignores the size of the global opportunity and India’s readiness to capture it. 
 This Indian fastidiousness is in sharp contrast to American extravagance: Anthropic has declared that, at over $30 trillion, its total addressable market is as large as the US economy. 
 The notion that the world’s enterprises will directly engage Anthropic or any other AI company to handle their IT work is absurd. They will continue to need services companies—and unless their current Indian vendors satisfy the new productivity and cost requirements, the business will flow to new ones that can. 
 As Tech Mahindra’s Mohit Joshi says , “...this AI deflation is way overdone. The reality is that clients are expecting productivity from AI, but this is maybe slightly different in terms of magnitude. But this is no different from the productivity that clients were earlier expecting from consolidation, that they were expecting from agile, that they were expecting it from sort of simplification, and then from automation, and now from AI.” 
 Some Indian IT majors might indeed be in the “luxury of the city” phase, although I doubt the best of them are. It is more likely that they are caught in the legacy trap: existing multi-year contracts that can be delivered with adjustments to existing delivery models. 
 Looking at what some CEOs are saying, this is perhaps the mechanism underlying AI revenue deflation. It is easy to advocate change, but cutting bonuses, freezing hiring or laying off tens of thousands of people is something that few Indian business leaders have ever had to do. 
 In Khaldun’s calculus, you have to become your own barbarian in order not to be upstaged by a new one. This not only means setting up units that will cannibalize your legacy business, but also through markets around the world. That is the kind of noise that foreign investors will hear loud and clear. 
 The author is co-founder and director of The Takshashila Institution, an independent centre for research and education in public policy.
